scenarios.title: The flickering kitchen
scenarios.setting: 7:42 AM. First call of the day. The work order says: "Kitchen lights flicker, and sometimes the toaster trips everything."

beats.scene: You pull up in the van. The homeowner meets you at the door and starts telling you about her cousin who "almost fixed it" last summer.
beats.prompt: First move?

choices.text: Ask when it happens: which lights, which outlets, what else is running
choices.outcome: Two minutes of questions just saved you an hour of guessing. Flickering lights and a tripping toaster on the same wall usually means one circuit with a problem, and now you know which wall.

choices.text: Head straight for the breaker panel
choices.outcome: You'll end up there anyway, but without her story you're testing blind. Most of the older guys will tell you the same thing: the house talks, let it.

choices.text: Start unscrewing the nearest outlet
choices.outcome: You don't know which circuit is sick yet, and that outlet is still live. Slow down. This trade hurts people who rush.

beats.scene: The breaker panel. Breaker #14 is warm to the touch. The faded label says "KITCHEN + ???".
beats.prompt: A warm breaker. What now?

choices.text: Kill the circuit, lock it out, then start opening things up
choices.outcome: Lockout first, every time. Warm means heat somewhere it shouldn't be, probably a loose connection or an overload. Now you can go find it without betting your hands on it.

choices.text: Flip it off and on to see if it resets
choices.outcome: She already tried that. Resetting a symptom finds nothing, and every minute that loose joint stays energized it cooks a little more.

choices.text: Clamp a meter on it while it's running to read the load
choices.outcome: Good instinct, real numbers beat guessing. But a warm breaker gets made safe before it gets measured. Order of operations matters more than the reading.

beats.scene: Junction box above the cabinets. One wire nut is browned, and the copper under it is dull and scorched.
beats.prompt: There's your heat. The homeowner is watching. "Is it bad?"

choices.text: Show her the scorched joint and explain it plainly
choices.outcome: "This connection was loose. Loose runs hot, and hot can start fires. I'm replacing it." No drama, no jargon. Customers call that guy back for everything.

choices.text: Say "yep, found it" and keep working
choices.outcome: The repair will be fine. But she never saw the problem, so she'll never understand what she paid for, and she won't remember your name next time something buzzes.

choices.text: Tell her the whole house probably needs rewiring
choices.outcome: You've seen one box. Maybe she does need more work, but you can't know that yet, and customers can smell a scare pitch from the driveway.

beats.scene: It's 11:50 and your 1:00 is across town. You could cut back to clean copper and do it right, or re-nut the old scorched ends and roll 20 minutes sooner.
beats.prompt: What do you do?

choices.text: Cut back to clean copper, re-strip, new connectors
choices.outcome: Scorched copper is brittle and oxidized. Twist a new nut onto it and you've rebuilt the exact fault you drove out here to fix. Do it once, do it right, eat the 20 minutes.

choices.text: Re-nut the old ends and book a follow-up visit
choices.outcome: Half those follow-ups never happen. Until it does, there's a known fire risk sitting in a ceiling with your name on the invoice under it.

choices.text: Call the 1:00 and say you'll be 20 minutes late
choices.outcome: Honest, and it works. Worth noticing though: the real decision was about the repair, not the calendar. Protect the work first and the schedule sorts itself out.

beats.scene: Done. Lights steady, breaker cool, and the panel now says "KITCHEN LIGHTS + COUNTER WEST" in your handwriting.
beats.prompt: Last five minutes on site. What matters most?

choices.text: Test everything in front of her, then write up what you found and fixed
choices.outcome: Flip every switch while she watches, then put it in writing. She remembers the demo, the paperwork covers you both, and that panel label will save the next electrician an hour.

choices.text: Pack fast and text the office you're rolling
choices.outcome: Efficient, but she never got to see it work. People pay for working lights. They tip, review, and refer because somebody showed them.

choices.text: Leave the old scorched bits in the junction box
choices.outcome: Loose debris in a box is a code violation, and it turns into a mystery for whoever opens it in ten years. Leave it cleaner than you found it.

scenarios.debrief: That was one call out of five today. The real job is half detective, half craftsman. Your hands make the fix, but your questions find it. If the scorched wire moment made you want to keep hunting, the apprenticeship is four years of exactly that, and you get paid from day one.

scenarios.title: Friday night on the line
scenarios.setting: 6:04 PM. You're on the hot line. The printer just woke up, and it's not going back to sleep until 9.

beats.prompt: Three tickets, one of you on the hot line. What fires first?

choices.text: Salmon first, then ribeye, then carbonara
choices.outcome: Longest cook goes down first so all three hit the pass hot at the same time. Cooks run that countdown in their heads a hundred times a night without thinking about it.

choices.text: Carbonara, it's the fastest. Clear it off the board
choices.outcome: And now it sits under the lamp for six minutes while the proteins catch up. Clearing tickets feels good. Serving cold pasta doesn't.

choices.text: Ribeye, steaks are the money dish
choices.outcome: The steak was never in trouble. The salmon table just inherited three extra minutes of waiting for no reason. Cook time sets the order, not the menu price.

beats.prompt: Two more tickets just dropped. Your move?

choices.text: Start the risotto now, the burger can wait
choices.outcome: An 18 minute dish is already late the second it prints. Get it on the heat. Everything else on this board can bend around it. The risotto can't bend.

choices.text: Knock out the burger first, it's easy
choices.outcome: The burger takes five minutes and was never in danger. You just turned the risotto into the apology you'll be making at 6:40.

choices.text: Ask the front to slow the seating down
choices.outcome: That lever is real, but you pull it when the kitchen is actually going down. It's 6 PM on a Friday. This is just the rush, and you can still win this board.

beats.prompt: The salmon's done a minute early. Its table's ribeye needs three more. Same table.

choices.text: Rest the salmon, plate both when the steak's ready
choices.outcome: A short rest is good for the fish anyway, and the table gets both plates hot at the same time. Half a table never leaves the pass. House rule in every kitchen that's any good.

choices.text: Send the salmon now while it's perfect
choices.outcome: So one person eats while their date sits there watching. Nobody remembers a perfect sear. Everybody remembers eating alone.

choices.text: Fire a fresh salmon timed to the steak
choices.outcome: Great timing, one wasted fish, twelve more minutes of grill space gone. A tasting menu kitchen might do it. On a Friday rush it buries you.

beats.prompt: New ticket, flagged allergy, right in the middle of the rush.

choices.text: Full stop. Confirm with the server, fresh pan, clean board, separate tongs
choices.outcome: Allergy tickets stop the line. Fresh pan, clean board, clean tongs, and you check with the server before anything touches heat. One slip here can put a guest in the ER. Every real kitchen treats this as sacred.

choices.text: Use the pasta station's usual pan, rinsed well
choices.outcome: Rinsed is not clean to an immune system. There are corners you can cut at 6:30 on a Friday. This is never one of them.

choices.text: Tell the server the kitchen can't do it safely tonight
choices.outcome: Safer than winging it, and sometimes it's the right call. But a kitchen that knows its allergy protocol cold can feed this table. Knowing it cold is the actual skill.

beats.prompt: 7:50. One ticket riding, your station looks like a crime scene, and the 8:15 wave is coming.

choices.text: Clean and restock the station while the well-done rides
choices.outcome: A well-done steak just handed you four free minutes. Wipe down, restock, reset. The 8:15 wave hits a clean station and you look like you're moving in slow motion while everyone else drowns.

choices.text: Lean on the pass and catch your breath
choices.outcome: You earned it. Problem is, the next wave shows up whether your station is ready or not. The good cooks rest after the reset, not before.

choices.text: Start playing with a special idea for tomorrow
choices.outcome: The creative side of cooking is real, and it happens at 2 PM with the radio on, not mid-service with a wave coming. Wrong twenty minutes for it.

scenarios.debrief: That was two hours squeezed into two minutes. The real job is running those fire times in your head, on your feet, in the heat, every single night. If the board filling up felt like a game you wanted to win, kitchens will feel like home. If it just stressed you out, trust that feeling. That's exactly what this preview is for.

scenarios.title: The built-in that has to fit
scenarios.setting: 8:10 AM. Install day for a custom built-in bookshelf you spent two weeks building in the shop. The pieces are prefinished walnut, and the alcove it goes into has exactly zero spare room.

beats.scene: The client's living room, drop cloths down, morning light through the window. The empty alcove sits between the chimney and the wall, and your truck outside is full of finished cabinet boxes.
beats.prompt: You measured this alcove three weeks ago. First move?

choices.text: Measure the alcove again: top, middle, bottom, and check for plumb
choices.outcome: Top reads a quarter inch narrower than your old number. Walls move, tape slips, somebody painted since you were here. Every installer who's been burned once measures the hole again before anything comes off the truck.

choices.text: Carry the boxes in first so you can see the whole picture
choices.outcome: Fair enough, you'll need them inside anyway. But now there's a hundred pounds of finished walnut leaning on the client's couch while you find out whether it even fits.

choices.text: Trust your numbers, you took them yourself
choices.outcome: You dry-fit the first box and it jams a foot short of home. Three weeks of paint and settling changed the opening, and finding that out with the cabinet wedged in the hole is the expensive way to find out.

beats.scene: Your level is held against the chimney side of the alcove. The bubble is off, and a tape check confirms it: the opening is three eighths of an inch narrower at the top than at the floor.
beats.prompt: The wall leans. The cabinet doesn't. What's the fix?

choices.text: Scribe the side panel: trace the wall's lean onto it, cut to match
choices.outcome: You run a compass down the wall, transfer the taper to the panel, and cut to the line. The cabinet now meets the crooked wall like they grew together. Scribing is half of what separates finish carpenters from everyone else.

choices.text: Set the cabinet plumb and cover the tapered gap with a filler strip
choices.outcome: It'll work, and plenty of kitchens get done exactly this way. But a tapered filler on a feature wall reads as a patch, and this client is paying custom money for custom lines.

choices.text: Muscle it in, the carcass will flex that much
choices.outcome: It goes in with a groan and now the face frame is racked, the doors won't sit flush, and you've stressed every joint you glued in the shop. Wood takes notes when you force it.

beats.scene: Sawhorses on the lawn, track saw out. On them sits the countertop piece: one slab of figured walnut, finished on all faces. There is no second slab. It needs to be cut to the exact width of the alcove.
beats.prompt: One board, one chance. How do you cut it?

choices.text: Cut it a strong sixteenth fat, test fit, shave down until it slides home
choices.outcome: Three trips between the alcove and the saw, and the final fit is snug enough to hold itself. You can always take more off. Nobody has ever put it back on.

choices.text: Make a cardboard template of the opening first, then cut to the template
choices.outcome: A template works, and for a weird multi-angle opening it's the right call. Here it mostly adds twenty minutes to a straight cut you still have to sneak up on at the end.

choices.text: Cut right to the tape number in one clean pass
choices.outcome: The number was right, the pencil line had width, and the blade took its kerf on the wrong side. The slab drops in with a gap you could lose a quarter in, and there's no spare walnut within two hundred miles.

beats.scene: The homeowner stands in the doorway with coffee, watching the cabinet come together. She points at the blank wall beside it and asks if you could add two floating shelves over there, since you're already here.
beats.prompt: Mid-install, new request. What do you tell her?

choices.text: Say yes, then price it: matched walnut, shop finish, a return visit
choices.outcome: You pull up the material cost on your phone, give her a number and a date, and she books it on the spot. Extra work from a happy client on site is the cheapest lead you'll ever get, as long as it goes on paper.

choices.text: Politely decline, today is scoped and you want to finish strong
choices.outcome: Nothing wrong with protecting the job in front of you. You did just leave money and a future referral standing in the doorway, though. A two minute quote would have kept both.

choices.text: Knock them out today with plywood from the van
choices.outcome: Van plywood next to figured walnut looks exactly like van plywood next to figured walnut. She'll stare at the mismatch for years, and it has your name on it.

beats.scene: The built-in stands in the alcove, scribed tight, countertop seated. Your drill is loaded and the stud finder marks are penciled on the back wall. Last step: fixing it in place for good.
beats.prompt: Time to fasten it. What matters here?

choices.text: Shim it dead level first, screw into studs, then check every door swing
choices.outcome: Level before fastening, because screws lock in whatever you've got. You hit four studs, the doors land flush, and the client runs a hand along the scribe line without finding it. Take the photos, this one goes in the portfolio.

choices.text: It's wedged in tight, a bead of construction adhesive will hold it
choices.outcome: It probably would hold. But a full-height cabinet that a kid can climb gets mechanical fasteners into framing, full stop. Adhesive is a helper, not the anchor.

choices.text: Drywall anchors, fast and done, you can't always find studs
choices.outcome: Anchors in half-inch drywall holding a loaded bookshelf is how furniture ends up on the evening news. Finding studs is the job, not an optional extra.

scenarios.debrief: One install, maybe six real decisions, and most of them happened before the first screw went in. Carpentry pays you for judgment with a saw in your hand: knowing when to re-measure, when to scribe, when to walk back to the truck instead of forcing it. If sneaking up on that walnut cut sounded satisfying instead of terrifying, look at trade school or an apprenticeship, and start a project portfolio now. Photos of clean work open more doors than any resume.

scenarios.title: One block of aluminum
scenarios.setting: 7:00 AM in the model shop. An engineer needs a sensor housing machined for a fit check on Thursday. You have the drawing, the CAD file, and exactly one billet of 6061 aluminum.

beats.scene: The drawing is clipped to the board above your bench: a small housing with a center bore, four mounting holes, and tolerance callouts in the corner blocks. One bore is flagged at plus or minus half a thou.
beats.prompt: Fresh print in hand. Where do you start?

choices.text: Read the whole print, then ask the engineer about that half-thou bore
choices.outcome: Turns out a bearing presses into that bore, so the tolerance is real and the engineer is glad you asked. Ten minutes with the print now beats finding a surprise callout with the part half machined.

choices.text: Start roughing the outside profile while you study the details
choices.outcome: Roughing is low risk and the clock is ticking, so plenty of machinists would. But if the print holds a surprise about stock orientation or datum faces, you may have just machined away your reference.

choices.text: Half a thou on a prototype is overkill, machine it to a loose thou
choices.outcome: The bearing press-fits loose, the fit check fails, and Thursday's meeting happens without a working part. You don't get to edit the print from the spindle. If a number looks wrong, somebody with the authority to change it has to say so.

beats.scene: The billet is clamped in the mill vise, and a dial indicator is mounted in the spindle. The CAM program is loaded on the control, cursor blinking on cycle start.
beats.prompt: Program's loaded. Do you hit go?

choices.text: Indicate the vise, verify your work zero, then dry run above the part
choices.outcome: The dry run shows a rapid move that would have grazed the clamp. You nudge the clearance plane, run it again clean, and now cycle start is a decision instead of a gamble. Setup is where good parts are actually made.

choices.text: Run the first part slow, feed override down, hand on feed hold
choices.outcome: A careful first run catches a lot, and every shop does it. It just catches problems while the tool is already in the metal, which is a worse time to learn about them than an air pass.

choices.text: Hit cycle start at 100%, this machine ran fine all week
choices.outcome: The work offset was still set from Tuesday's job. The end mill buries itself half an inch off target, snaps, and your one billet now has a gouge through the mounting boss. The machine did exactly what it was told.

beats.scene: The part sits in the vise, warm from cutting, with the center bore freshly opened. Your bore gauge reads one thousandth under the target diameter.
beats.prompt: The bore is a thou undersize. Next move?

choices.text: Let it cool, re-measure, then take a light spring pass and check again
choices.outcome: Cool, it measures seven tenths under, because warm aluminum lies to a gauge. Two light passes later you're inside the half-thou window. Sneaking up on a tight bore is slow on purpose.

choices.text: Grab the senior machinist to confirm your measurement first
choices.outcome: A second set of eyes on a tight tolerance never hurts, and she confirms your reading. She also points out the part is still warm, which you could have caught yourself. Ask when you're stuck, measure cold either way.

choices.text: A thou under, close enough, move to the next feature
choices.outcome: The tolerance was plus or minus half a thou, so the part is scrap the moment you walk away from it. The bearing won't seat, and 'close' doesn't appear anywhere on the inspection sheet.

beats.scene: Your bench monitor shows the CAD model next to the paper drawing. The print calls the mounting holes at 42 millimeters apart. You measure the model: 44. They cannot both be right.
beats.prompt: The drawing and the CAD disagree. Which do you machine?

choices.text: Stop and ask the engineer which one governs before drilling anything
choices.outcome: The engineer swears, checks, and tells you the CAD is current and the print never got revved. Thirty seconds of asking just saved the fit check, and now the print gets fixed so the next guy doesn't hit the same trap.

choices.text: Follow the print, drawings govern in most shops
choices.outcome: That's the textbook rule and nobody would fire you for it. But in prototype work the model is often newer than the paper, and a known conflict you didn't flag is still your problem when the holes don't line up Thursday.

choices.text: Go with the CAD, it's obviously the newer file
choices.outcome: You guessed, and this time you happened to guess right, which is worse than it sounds. The day the guess goes the other way, four holes in the wrong place turn your only billet into a paperweight.

beats.scene: The finished housing sits on the granite surface plate next to your micrometer and bore gauge. It looks done. The engineer is already hovering by the shop door.
beats.prompt: Part's off the machine. What does 'done' mean?

choices.text: Deburr, check every callout against the print, write the numbers down
choices.outcome: You hand over the part with a filled-in dimension sheet and a note about the print error. The engineer trusts the next part you make before you've made it. That reputation is most of what a model maker gets paid for.

choices.text: Hand it straight over, engineering has their own inspection gear
choices.outcome: They can measure it, sure. But if anything is off, they find out in their lab instead of ten feet from your machine, and the rework loop that could have taken an hour now takes a day.

choices.text: Skip deburring, it's a prototype, nobody's grading the edges
choices.outcome: The engineer slices a finger on a razor burr during the fit check, and the sharp edge also keeps the housing from seating flat. Burrs are not cosmetic. They change how parts sit, seal, and handle.

scenarios.debrief: A model maker lives in that gap between a drawing and a thing you can hold, and most of the craft is checking twice before doing anything you can't undo. The machines are the fun part. The discipline around them is the actual job. The usual way in is high school plus on-the-job training or an apprenticeship, and a few photographed builds made from real prints will say more about you than any application form.

scenarios.title: The client thinks it's boring
scenarios.setting: 10:05 AM at the studio. You're rebranding a three-location coffee chain. Round one feedback landed overnight, and the final presentation is Friday.

beats.scene: Your monitor shows the client's email next to your logo presentation. The email reads: 'Honestly it feels a bit boring? We want FUN. Also my nephew mocked something up, attached.' The nephew's file is a gradient wordmark in a bubble font.
beats.prompt: That email. What do you actually do with it?

choices.text: Book a 20 minute call to find out what 'boring' means to them
choices.outcome: On the call it comes out in one sentence: their competitor just rebranded loud and bright, and they're scared of looking stale next door. Now you have a design problem instead of an adjective, and those are solvable.

choices.text: Crank out three 'fun' variations and send them over by lunch
choices.outcome: Fast and agreeable, and sometimes volume shakes something loose. But you're treating the symptom. Without knowing what's driving the note, you're guessing three times instead of once.

choices.text: Reply with a long defense of the original concept
choices.outcome: Every point in your essay is correct and the client reads it as 'the designer thinks we're dumb.' Nobody has ever been argued into loving a logo over email. You just made Friday harder.

beats.scene: Video call. The client has the competitor's new website up on a shared screen: neon colors, chunky type, everywhere. She asks, half joking, if your design could 'do that.'
beats.prompt: They want to chase the competitor. Your move?

choices.text: Show both brands side by side, pitch energy in color and layouts
choices.outcome: You sketch it live: the sturdy logo stays, but the posters, cups, and Instagram grid get a loud secondary palette. She sees her shop looking current without copying the place across the street. That reframe is the actual job.

choices.text: Agree to fully explore a louder direction alongside the current one
choices.outcome: Defensible, and clients like feeling heard. It also just doubled your workload before a Friday deadline, and a direction built on 'be like them' tends to die in round three anyway.

choices.text: Promise a brand new logo concept by Friday
choices.outcome: A logo rebuilt in three panicked days to spite a competitor will look exactly like that. You've also taught the client that one nervous email resets the whole project.

beats.scene: Wednesday, 6:40 PM. Your artboard is a mess of two half-finished directions: the refined original with the new loud applications, and a second, riskier layout system. Friday is not moving.
beats.prompt: Two days left, two half-done directions. What ships?

choices.text: Kill the second direction, polish one story fully with real mockups
choices.outcome: One direction, executed all the way down to the cup sleeve, lands harder than two maybes. Choosing what dies is a craft skill. The folder of killed concepts is where every working designer's hard drive goes to grieve.

choices.text: Present both at 70% and let the client pick a lane
choices.outcome: Honest about where things stand, and some clients handle it fine. But clients buy confidence, and 70% work invites feedback on the unfinished parts instead of decisions on the finished ones.

choices.text: All-nighter both, plus a third safe option just in case
choices.outcome: You arrive Friday wrecked, presenting three mediocre decks instead of one good one. More options reads as less conviction, and the client can hear it in your voice by slide four.

beats.scene: A type foundry's website is open on your screen. The display face the client flipped for in round one costs $600 for a commercial license. The project's font budget, per the contract, is zero.
beats.prompt: They love a font the budget can't buy. What now?

choices.text: Tell them the cost and show a close open-source alternative beside it
choices.outcome: You send both options with the price tag visible. They squint at the comparison, decide the free one is 95% of the vibe, and you've shown them you treat their money like your own. Some clients pay the $600. Their call to make.

choices.text: Quietly swap in the free lookalike and present only that
choices.outcome: The deck looks great and nobody asks. But if she ever compares it to round one and spots the switch, you look sneaky over $600, and trust is the only thing keeping a freelance client around.

choices.text: Use the font anyway, foundries never check small clients
choices.outcome: Foundries absolutely check, and the scary letter goes to your client, not to you. You put her tiny coffee chain on the hook for a licensing claim to save yourself one awkward conversation.

beats.scene: Friday. The conference room screen shows your opening slide: the new mark on a coffee cup in someone's hand, steam rising, the loud new poster wall blurred behind it. The client and her two partners are seated.
beats.prompt: How do you run this room?

choices.text: Walk them through it in context, tying every choice back to the stale fear
choices.outcome: Cup, storefront, Instagram grid, each one answering the worry she told you on Tuesday's call. By the time the logo appears alone on a slide, it's already theirs. Presenting the thinking is half the deliverable.

choices.text: Send the PDF the night before so they arrive with reactions ready
choices.outcome: Some clients genuinely prefer it. You also just let three people form opinions alone at midnight without you there to answer the first 'hmm,' and first impressions don't get a second take.

choices.text: Show all twelve explorations so they can see the effort
choices.outcome: Forty minutes later the partners are debating option seven versus option eleven, two versions you already know are weak. You brought a buffet to people who hired you to cook.

scenarios.debrief: Most days in this job are exactly that: translating a nervous email into a design problem, killing work you liked, and defending the client's money along with their brand. The craft gets you hired. The listening keeps you hired. You don't need a design degree to start, you need two or three case studies that show this kind of thinking, so invent a client if you have to and document every decision.

scenarios.title: Episode four shoots today
scenarios.setting: 9:00 AM in your apartment studio corner. You're four episodes into a six-part series, and episode three underperformed hard. Today you shoot and edit episode four.

beats.scene: Your laptop shows the analytics dashboard for episode three. The retention graph starts at 100% and falls off a cliff at the eight second mark, then flattens into a long slow bleed. The comment count is weirdly fine.
beats.prompt: Episode three flopped. What do you do with that before shooting four?

choices.text: Find the exact second people left, rewatch it, fix that in today's script
choices.outcome: You scrub to 0:08 and there it is: you're still saying hello while the hook from the title hasn't appeared yet. People gave you eight seconds and you spent them on throat clearing. Today's script now opens inside the payoff.

choices.text: Read through the comments to get a feel for what landed
choices.outcome: Comments tell you what your fans think, and your fans already stayed. The 70% who left at eight seconds never comment. Vibes from the survivors won't explain the cliff.

choices.text: Scrap the series format and chase the trend all over your feed today
choices.outcome: One soft episode and you torched a four-episode investment to copy a trend that peaks before you can even post. Four episodes of audience momentum, traded for a panic move.

beats.scene: Camera on the tripod, key light on, you in frame on the monitor. The script's first line is taped below the lens. Record is one button away.
beats.prompt: How do you shoot the opening?

choices.text: Shoot three different cold opens and pick the winner in the edit
choices.outcome: Thirty seconds of frame one decides more than the other seven minutes combined, so you give the edit three candidates: the bold claim, the result shown first, the question. Future you at the timeline will know which one works. Present you can't.

choices.text: Drill one hook until the delivery is perfect
choices.outcome: Craft matters and take nine is genuinely good. But you polished one guess. A flawless delivery of the wrong opening still dies at eight seconds.

choices.text: Open with 'hey guys, welcome back, before we start today...'
choices.outcome: That's the exact eight seconds that killed episode three, back for a rematch. Nobody new knows you, so 'welcome back' is spoken to people already gone.

beats.scene: Mid-take. Through the window behind you, a neighbor drags a lawnmower across his yard. Your headphone check confirms it: a low growl sitting under every word on the shotgun mic.
beats.prompt: Mower in the audio, schedule's tight. Keep rolling?

choices.text: Stop. Wait it out or move setups, and get clean audio
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes lost, clean track gained. Viewers forgive soft focus, weird framing, even bad lighting. Bad audio gets a swipe inside two seconds, every time, and no amount of editing charm survives it.

choices.text: Keep rolling and plan to scrub it with noise removal in post
choices.outcome: Modern denoisers are good, and on a flat hum they're great. A mower pitching up and down under your voice leaves that underwater artifact sound, and you won't know how bad until you're already in the edit with no reshoot time.

choices.text: Ignore it, the visuals carry this episode anyway
choices.outcome: The edit sounds like you filmed inside a blender and now the whole shoot day is a reshoot. No one has ever watched a video for the visuals while hating the sound.

beats.scene: Night. Your editing timeline glows in the dark room, a rough cut reading 11:42 in the duration counter. Your best performing episodes all live around seven minutes. There's a three minute tangent in the middle that makes you laugh every time.
beats.prompt: The cut is 11:42. Your winners run seven. What goes?

choices.text: Cut everything that doesn't pay off the title, tangent included
choices.outcome: The tangent fights you all the way out, and the cut lands at 7:10 feeling twice as fast. Save the clip, it might be its own short. The episode made a promise in the title, and every second either serves that promise or stalls it.

choices.text: Keep it near eleven but tighten every pause and dead frame
choices.outcome: Pace editing is a real skill and the cut does feel faster. But you kept three minutes of detour because it was fun to make, and the retention graph doesn't grade your fun.

choices.text: Keep everything, the tangent is the best part
choices.outcome: Best part for you. The graph will show a slide starting right where the episode forgets its own title, and the algorithm reads that slide as a reason to stop recommending you.

beats.scene: Export finished. Your screen shows the upload page: empty title field, empty thumbnail slot, and your series schedule note that says episodes post Thursdays at 5 PM. It's Wednesday, 11:30 PM.
beats.prompt: Last call: title, thumbnail, timing. How do you package it?

choices.text: Title and thumbnail state the payoff, post in the usual series slot
choices.outcome: The thumbnail shows the result, the title promises it, and second one of the video delivers it, so the click and the content agree. Posting in the usual slot keeps the series audience trained. Packaging is part of the edit, not an afterthought.

choices.text: Post it now, it's done and momentum is momentum
choices.outcome: Shipping beats sitting on it, true. But your audience learned Thursdays at five, midnight Wednesday hits them asleep, and the first hour of a video's life weighs more than any other hour it will ever have.

choices.text: Run a shock thumbnail and title the video doesn't actually deliver
choices.outcome: Click-through spikes, retention craters at the moment people realize the bait, and the platform reads that pattern exactly for what it is. You spent audience trust to rent one afternoon of numbers.

scenarios.debrief: That's the loop: read the data without flinching, shoot with the edit in mind, cut the parts only you love, package honestly, repeat on schedule. The camera is maybe a third of this job. No one will ask for your credentials, they'll ask for your channel, so the move is to start a small series now, track what the retention graph tells you, and let the published work be the application.

scenarios.title: The checkout nobody finishes
scenarios.setting: 9:30 AM standup at a mid-size shopping app. Checkout completion dropped four points last month, a VP has opinions, and you're the designer on the fix.

beats.scene: A conference room. Your PM stands at the whiteboard where he's drawn a progress bar with a smiley face at the end, and the words 'SHIP THIS' underlined twice. The checkout funnel chart on the TV behind him shows a cliff at step three.
beats.prompt: The PM hands you a solution, not a problem. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask what evidence points at progress anxiety, pull the funnel data
choices.outcome: The data shows users bailing at step three specifically, which a progress bar doesn't explain. The PM's idea came from a podcast. You're not fighting him, you're moving the conversation from a guess to a question you can answer.

choices.text: Mock the progress bar fast so there's something concrete to react to
choices.outcome: A quick mock does make discussions real, and it keeps the PM feeling heard. The risk is the mock becomes the plan by default, and you've now spent a day decorating a hypothesis nobody checked.

choices.text: Just build it as specced, he's the PM
choices.outcome: Three weeks later the progress bar ships, the funnel doesn't move, and the question in the retro is why design didn't catch it. Taking orders without looking at the problem is how the role shrinks into a mockup vending machine.

beats.scene: Your desk, headphones on. Five session recordings play in a grid: in four of them, the cursor reaches the shipping address field, the autocomplete suggests the wrong apartment, and the user retypes the address three times before quitting.
beats.prompt: The real snag is the address field, not progress. What do you take back?

choices.text: Bring the clips to the PM, propose fixing the field first
choices.outcome: Thirty seconds of a real user fighting that field does what no slide deck can. The PM winces at clip two and the roadmap quietly reorders itself. Evidence you can watch beats evidence you have to believe.

choices.text: Design both the field fix and the progress bar, let him choose
choices.outcome: Diplomatic, and both might even ship someday. But presenting them as equals tells the PM the evidence is a coin flip, and you know it isn't. Part of this job is having a recommendation.

choices.text: Quietly design what the data says and unveil it at the review
choices.outcome: The review opens with the PM asking where his progress bar went, and now the meeting is about the ambush instead of the users. Being right in secret buys you nothing.

beats.scene: Design review. Your new address flow is on the big screen. The VP of Product leans back and says he hates multi-step forms, everything should be one page, that's how the app he used at his last company did it.
beats.prompt: VP opinion versus your test evidence. How do you play it?

choices.text: Ask what outcome he's after, then offer to test his one-pager against yours
choices.outcome: He wants fewer abandons, same as you, so you propose a quick unmoderated test of both. He agrees because who argues against evidence they might win. Now a prototype settles it instead of rank.

choices.text: Take the note and build the one-page version he asked for
choices.outcome: Low friction today, and sometimes picking battles is wisdom. But you watched users succeed with the stepped flow, and the long single page is where mobile forms go to die. The abandons will come back wearing his idea.

choices.text: Agree in the meeting, then ship your version anyway
choices.outcome: He opens the app a month later and sees the thing he said no to. Whatever credibility the research bought you is gone, and every future review now comes with a VP checking your homework.

beats.scene: A small research room, your prototype on a test phone. The participant is on the address step, thumb hovering, brow furrowed. The silence stretches past ten seconds and your leg is bouncing under the table.
beats.prompt: She's stuck in silence. What do you do?

choices.text: Stay quiet, let her struggle, ask afterward what she expected to happen
choices.outcome: She eventually taps the wrong thing, which is the single most useful moment of your week. Her struggle is the data. In production there will be no designer sitting next to anyone.

choices.text: Gently ask what she's thinking right now
choices.outcome: A think-aloud nudge is standard practice and gets you words. It also pulls her out of real behavior into performing an answer, so time the nudge late, not the first moment silence gets uncomfortable.

choices.text: Jump in and show her where the button is
choices.outcome: You just rescued your design instead of testing it. The session ends happy and tells you nothing, and the real users next month won't have you reaching over their shoulder.

beats.scene: Your engineer's desk, two mugs, her screen showing the ticket estimate: the address autocomplete service you designed around is three sprints of integration work. The release train leaves in one.
beats.prompt: The ideal version doesn't fit the deadline. What ships?

choices.text: Design the fallback: solid manual entry now, autocomplete next release
choices.outcome: You sit with her and spec every state of the plain form: errors, edge cases, keyboard types. Users get a real fix this release instead of a perfect one next quarter, and the autocomplete lands later on solid ground. Shipping in steps is still shipping.

choices.text: Push to delay the release until the full version is ready
choices.outcome: Sometimes worth it, and at least it's honest about quality. But users keep fighting the broken field for two extra months, and you spent political capital a lighter solution didn't need.

choices.text: Hand off the ideal mocks and let engineering sort out the gaps
choices.outcome: She improvises the error states at 11 PM before code freeze, and the result has your name on it in the design review. Undesigned states don't stay undesigned. They just get designed by whoever is most tired.

scenarios.debrief: Notice how little of that was drawing screens. Product design is mostly steering decisions with evidence: watching real people, translating opinions into testable questions, and designing the version that can actually ship. If sitting on your hands while that participant struggled sounded doable, you'd survive the job. Entry is portfolio-first, so build one honest end-to-end case study, including what the feedback made you change, and it will beat a degree listing every time.

scenarios.title: When the model is wrong
scenarios.setting: 10:00 AM at a startup building a document workspace. Your assignment: design the new AI summary feature. The model demo looked magical yesterday. Your job is everything the demo skipped.

beats.scene: A glass-walled meeting room. The PM replays yesterday's demo on the TV: a 40 page contract collapsing into a tidy five bullet summary in seconds. He says the plan is to ship the happy path now and handle errors in a fast follow.
beats.prompt: 'Ship the happy path, errors later.' Your response?

choices.text: Ask how often the model misses, and design the failure states from day one
choices.outcome: The ML lead admits the summary is off in maybe one of ten documents. At that rate the error state is a core screen, not an edge case. For AI features, what happens when it's wrong is most of the design surface.

choices.text: Agree to sequence it: happy path first, failure states as backlog tickets
choices.outcome: Pragmatic, and at least the gaps are written down. But fast follows have a way of becoming next quarter, and meanwhile real users meet a confident feature that is wrong every tenth time with nothing to catch them.

choices.text: Trust the model team to get accuracy high enough that errors barely matter
choices.outcome: No model team on earth will promise you that, and the first customer who forwards a wrong summary to their boss becomes a churn story with your feature's name in it. You can't design around a failure rate by hoping it shrinks.

beats.scene: Your Figma file, two frames side by side: the trigger button, and then a blank canvas labeled 'generating...' Engineering says a long document takes six to twelve seconds to summarize. That's an eternity of screen.
beats.prompt: Six to twelve seconds of nothing. What do you design into the wait?

choices.text: Stream the summary in as it generates, with a stop button the whole time
choices.outcome: Users see the first bullet inside two seconds, can start reading, and can bail the moment it's going sideways. Streaming turns dead air into a progress signal, and the stop button tells people the machine works for them.

choices.text: A skeleton loader with rotating status copy like 'reading section 3 of 9'
choices.outcome: Honest progress beats a spinner, and the copy buys patience. The user still gets nothing to read until second twelve though, and nothing to do if the output is already going wrong behind the curtain.

choices.text: A nice branded spinner, it's only a few seconds
choices.outcome: At second eight of a locked spinner, users decide the feature is broken and start mashing the button, queueing three more generations behind the first. An unexplained wait with no exit reads as a hang, every time.

beats.scene: Your test build, a real vendor contract loaded. The AI summary on screen states the contract renews on March 1. You search the document: March appears nowhere in it. The model invented the date, formatted beautifully.
beats.prompt: The summary states a date the document never mentions. What's the design answer?

choices.text: Ground every claim: tap a bullet, see the exact source lines highlighted
choices.outcome: Now a fabricated date is a bullet with no highlight behind it, visibly different from the real ones. You can't make the model stop inventing, so you make inventions catchable in one tap. Verification becomes part of reading, not homework.

choices.text: Add a persistent 'AI can make mistakes, verify important info' notice
choices.outcome: Industry standard, legally sensible, and worth having. But a disclaimer under every output protects the company more than the user. Day two, nobody sees it anymore, and the fake date still looks exactly as confident as the true ones.

choices.text: File it as a model bug and ask ML to fix hallucinations before launch
choices.outcome: The ML lead laughs, not unkindly. Hallucination is a property of these models, not a ticket. Designing as if someone will remove it means shipping a UI that lies with a straight face.

beats.scene: Whiteboard session, sketches everywhere. The open question in red marker: a user reads the summary and disagrees with bullet three. Right now the output is a sealed block of text with a thumbs-down button.
beats.prompt: The user thinks the output is wrong. What can they do about it?

choices.text: Make it editable with undo, and feedback that routes somewhere real
choices.outcome: The user fixes bullet three in five seconds, keeps the rest, and the edit gets logged as a labeled correction for the ML team. People trust output they're allowed to correct, and your model gets training signal for free.

choices.text: Add a regenerate button so they can roll for a better version
choices.outcome: Regenerate is table stakes and worth having. But it throws away the four bullets that were fine to re-gamble on the one that wasn't, and the user with a specific correction in their head still has nowhere to put it.

choices.text: Keep it locked, edits would compromise the AI-generated integrity
choices.outcome: So the user copies it into a doc to fix it there, and your feature just became a worse first draft button. A sealed output tells people to take it or leave it, and most of them pick leave.

beats.scene: The research call recording, paused. Your test participant just read a summary containing a planted error, nodded, said 'great, saves me reading all that,' and moved on. The citation feature sat right there, untouched.
beats.prompt: She trusted the wrong answer and never checked. What do you do with that?

choices.text: Treat it as a design failure: make verifying the default for high stakes
choices.outcome: You redesign the flow so high-stakes extractions, dates, amounts, obligations, surface their source line inline instead of behind a tap. If people only verify when verification is the path of least resistance, then that's the path you build.

choices.text: Make the disclaimer bigger and add an onboarding tip about checking sources
choices.outcome: A reasonable patch, and onboarding tips do move the numbers a little. But you watched a motivated participant skip a one-tap check with a researcher in the room. More words will not outwork that behavior in the wild.

choices.text: Note that users are careless and move on, you can't fix human nature
choices.outcome: That exact carelessness is the job you were hired for. Blaming the user is how a feature ends up in a screenshot thread titled 'the AI told me my contract renewed in March.'

scenarios.debrief: Almost none of that was about making the AI look cool. The craft is designing for a system that is usually right, confidently wrong sometimes, and never sure, so the user stays in control the whole way through. It's a young field, which means your portfolio can compete with anyone's. Build one case study of a generative flow with real loading, error, edit, and undo states, explain your trust decisions, and you're already speaking the language hiring managers are listening for.

scenarios.title: The handle that won't mold
scenarios.setting: 9:00 AM in the studio. The electric kettle you've been designing for a year is headed to tooling, and the manufacturer's feedback on your signature handle just landed in your inbox.

beats.scene: Your monitor: the manufacturer's DFM report open beside your kettle renders. The sweeping handle you fought for is circled in red with a note that its undercut needs a collapsible core, adding $40k in tooling and three weeks.
beats.prompt: Your signature handle just got flagged. First move?

choices.text: Call the toolmaker, understand the real constraint before changing anything
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes in, the toolmaker mentions that shifting the parting line and opening the curve by a few millimeters kills the undercut entirely. You can't negotiate with a constraint you haven't actually understood, and most of them have more give than the PDF suggests.

choices.text: Start reworking the handle in CAD today to remove the undercut
choices.outcome: Responsive, and the schedule will thank you. But you're redesigning against one sentence in a report, and you may be about to give away a curve the toolmaker could have saved with a smarter mold action.

choices.text: Escalate to keep the handle as-is, it's the whole identity of the product
choices.outcome: You win the meeting and the product loses $40k of margin before a single unit sells. A signature detail that sinks the business case gets remembered, just not the way you wanted.

beats.scene: Your CAD screen, the handle surfaces shaded in draft analysis mode, red zones glowing where the walls are too vertical to release from a mold. Adding the required two degrees of draft visibly changes the silhouette you've lived with for a year.
beats.prompt: The draft angles change your silhouette. How do you handle it?

choices.text: Rebuild the surfaces with draft designed in, print a model to judge
choices.outcome: Instead of a taxed version of the old curve, you make the draft part of a new curve, and the overnight print confirms it still feels right wrapped in a fist. Fold a constraint in this early and it becomes part of the design. Patch it in at the end and it always shows.

choices.text: Apply the minimum tweak and approve it from the renders
choices.outcome: The renders look close enough and the schedule stays happy. But a screen can't tell you what two degrees does to a palm, and this is a product people hold every morning before coffee.

choices.text: Slip the change through quietly and hope nobody compares prototypes
choices.outcome: The brand manager compares prototypes. Now the conversation is about why design hid a change instead of whether the change works, and your next ten decisions get double-checked.

beats.scene: The print lab bench. The revised handle, fresh off the printer in gray resin, is zip-tied to a weighted kettle body. In your hand it's fine. Full of water, the grip feels shallower than the original, like it might roll out of a loose grip.
beats.prompt: The revision feels worse full. What now?

choices.text: Print quick variants and put them in other people's hands
choices.outcome: You print three options overnight and watch five coworkers pour water with each. Two of them hold the kettle completely differently than you do, and variant B wins for every grip style. Your hand has held this project too long to be a fair judge.

choices.text: Trust your own read, you've held this product five hundred times
choices.outcome: Your calibration is real and often right. But five hundred holds also means you've adapted to its flaws, and the arthritis-handed customer pouring boiling water never got a vote.

choices.text: Call it done, the renders look right and the deadline is real
choices.outcome: A handle that feels insecure with a kilo of hot water in it is a return, a one-star review, or worse. Feel is the product in this category, and renders don't have hands.

beats.scene: The mechanical engineer's desk, a sectioned CAD view on screen. She needs the handle's wall thickness up half a millimeter for drop-test strength, and that extra plastic will pull sink marks into your glossy outer surface.
beats.prompt: Strength wants thick walls, gloss hates them. How do you resolve it?

choices.text: Work it with her: internal ribs for strength, keep the skin thin
choices.outcome: An hour at her desk trading sketches finds it: ribs inside the handle carry the drop load while the outer wall stays uniform, so the gloss survives. The engineer stops being the person who ruins your surfaces and starts being how your surfaces ship.

choices.text: Accept a matte texture across the handle to hide whatever sink appears
choices.outcome: Texture hiding sink is the oldest trick in injection molding, and it would ship fine. You've just spent a design decision covering a problem that an hour of engineering collaboration could have actually solved.

choices.text: Hold the gloss spec and tell her sink marks are manufacturing's problem
choices.outcome: First shots come out of the tool with shadowy dents down your beautiful gloss, exactly as predicted, and the fix now costs tool rework instead of a CAD session. The physics was never going to blink first.

beats.scene: The gate review room. On the table: your original concept model, the revised prototype, and the cost sheet. Around it: the product manager, the engineer, the brand lead. The revision is up for tooling approval today.
beats.prompt: Final review. How do you present the revision?

choices.text: Tell the change story: what moved, why, with both models to hold
choices.outcome: You pass the prototypes around the table and walk the room from the $40k undercut to the ribbed handle that pours better than the original. The revision reads as the design getting smarter, and the gate passes in forty minutes. Owning the tradeoffs is what makes them yours.

choices.text: Present polished renders of the final only, keep it forward-looking
choices.outcome: The renders are gorgeous and the meeting runs smooth, until the brand lead picks the old model off the shelf and asks what changed. Now you're explaining differences defensively that you could have narrated on your own terms.

choices.text: Present the original as 'option A' and try to relitigate the undercut
choices.outcome: The engineer's jaw tightens, the PM flips straight to the cost sheet, and the room relearns that your agreements don't stay agreed. The handle died weeks ago. Dragging it into the gate just costs you the room.

scenarios.debrief: Industrial design lives exactly there, in the push and pull between the form you can sketch and the object a factory can actually make a hundred thousand of. The designers who last treat molding constraints and engineers as material to work with, same as the plastic. A degree opens doors at the big brands, but a portfolio of real objects, with sketches, models, and honest notes on what manufacturing changed, is what gets you across the table.

scenarios.title: Ship it by Thursday
scenarios.setting: Monday, 9:15 AM at a 20-person startup. You are the design and front-end seat, both of them. The PM wants the new plan-upgrade flow live for Thursday's investor demo.

beats.scene: The PM at your desk, Slack open on his phone, the feature wishlist on your second monitor: upgrade modal, plan comparison table, annual toggle with a celebratory animation, promo code field. Thursday is circled on the wall calendar.
beats.prompt: Four features, three days, one of you. What do you commit to?

choices.text: Commit to the core upgrade path done well, everything else explicitly cut
choices.outcome: You and the PM agree on paper: modal, plan table, payment, done properly with real states. The toggle animation and promo field move to next week by name, not by silence. A small thing that works beats a big thing that almost does, especially in front of investors.

choices.text: Say yes to all of it and plan to make up the gap over the weekend
choices.outcome: The hero move, and sometimes at a startup it's genuinely the job. But a weekend of hero coding produces Thursday-morning bugs, and you've taught the PM that every wishlist fits in three days.

choices.text: Say yes in the moment and figure out what's real later
choices.outcome: Wednesday night the PM discovers the promo field doesn't exist, except he demos it to investors Thursday because nobody told him. A silent cut is just a surprise with a delay on it.

beats.scene: Your editor on one screen, the design system's Storybook on the other. The plan picker wants a segmented control. You scroll the component list twice: buttons, tabs, radio groups. No segmented control anywhere.
beats.prompt: The system doesn't have the component you need. What do you do?

choices.text: Compose it from system primitives, file an issue for the real one
choices.outcome: A radio group styled with existing tokens gets you 95% of a segmented control that inherits theming, dark mode, and focus states for free. The issue you file means the system grows from real need. That loop is basically the design engineer job description.

choices.text: Build a clean one-off component with a TODO to systematize later
choices.outcome: It ships and it looks right. It also hard-codes four color values that will quietly go stale at the next theme update, and that TODO is entering a graveyard with very few survivors.

choices.text: npm install a component library that has one ready to go
choices.outcome: One control just added 200kb of someone else's design decisions to the bundle, and its focus ring, spacing, and font all disagree with the rest of the app. You now maintain a dependency forever to avoid an afternoon of CSS.

beats.scene: Tuesday afternoon. The happy path works: pick a plan, pay, confetti. Your terminal shows the payment API's error list scrolling past: card declined, expired, timeout, rate limited. None of them have a designed screen.
beats.prompt: Happy path works. The failure cases are naked. Spend time there?

choices.text: Build the failure states now: declined, timeout, retry, in that order
choices.outcome: Declined cards are the most common thing that happens on a payment form after success, so you give it a clear message, a card-edit shortcut, and a retry that doesn't double-charge. This is the whole point of one person owning design and code: the sad paths get real design instead of leftovers.

choices.text: One generic 'something went wrong, try again' toast for everything
choices.outcome: It's honest coverage and it ships today. But a user whose card was declined and a user whose connection dropped need opposite advice, and your one toast shrugs at both of them.

choices.text: Skip it, the demo uses a test card that always succeeds
choices.outcome: The demo survives, then the feature goes live Friday because it's 'done,' and the first real declined card strands a paying customer on a frozen spinner.

beats.scene: Wednesday, 9:40 PM, the office empty. Two browser windows: the plan card's entrance animation at 90% smooth, and your accessibility checklist showing unchecked boxes for keyboard navigation, focus order, and contrast on the price text.
beats.prompt: One evening left. The animation or the a11y pass?

choices.text: Do the a11y pass. The animation ships at 90% or not at all
choices.outcome: Tab order gets fixed, focus rings land where eyes expect them, and the gray price text passes contrast. Nobody upgrades a plan because of an entrance animation, and somebody always tries to pay with a keyboard. The checkout working for everyone is the polish.

choices.text: Finish the animation, file the a11y pass as Friday's first ticket
choices.outcome: At least it's tracked, which is better than most teams manage. But Friday has its own fires, and you've put 'looks delightful' ahead of 'works for keyboard users' on a payment flow. You know which one that order serves.

choices.text: Neither, there's time to squeeze the promo code field back in
choices.outcome: Midnight delivers a half-tested promo field with no error states bolted onto an unaudited flow. You took Monday's careful scope cut and spent it on exactly the feature you cut, minus the care.

beats.scene: Thursday, 8:30 AM. The demo is at 10. On your MacBook, Safari shows the plan cards overlapping at tablet width, a flexbox gap bug Chrome quietly forgave all week. Your coffee has gone cold next to the trackpad.
beats.prompt: Layout bug in Safari, ninety minutes to demo. What's the move?

choices.text: Smallest targeted fix, then verify the whole flow in all three browsers
choices.outcome: One line swaps the gap for margins, and the full click-through in all three contexts takes ten minutes. You're done by 9:05 with time to breathe. Surgical under pressure, thorough right after: that's the rhythm this seat runs on.

choices.text: Demo in Chrome only, note the Safari bug for after
choices.outcome: Controlling the demo environment is legitimate, and plenty of launches have survived on it. You're one investor opening the link on an iPhone away from the bug presenting itself, on brand-new software, to exactly the wrong audience.

choices.text: This flexbox layout has bugged you all week, refactor it properly now
choices.outcome: The refactor touches eleven files, and at 9:50 you're debugging a new regression the old code never had. The proper rebuild was a good idea with a terrible timestamp. It belonged to Friday.

scenarios.debrief: That's the seat: you argue scope in the morning, extend the design system before lunch, and fix Safari with cold coffee at 8:30 AM, because the mockup and the production code are both yours. The range is the appeal and the pressure, same coin. Hiring for this role is portfolio-first and specific: show a feature you took from sketch to merged PR, with the error states and accessibility notes visible, and you'll stand out from every candidate who only brought mockups.

scenarios.title: Bed 12 keeps calling
scenarios.setting: 2:40 PM on a med-surg floor, hour nine of a twelve hour shift. You have four patients, and the man in bed 12 has pressed his call light three times in the last hour.

messages.name: MR. ALVAREZ, BED 12
messages.text: Can you stay a second? Everyone keeps saying the procedure is tomorrow and then leaving. What are they not telling me?

beats.prompt: He's scared and you have three other patients. What do you do?

choices.text: Pull up a chair and ask what he's heard so far
choices.outcome: He talks for ninety seconds and the real fear comes out: his brother had the same procedure and it went badly. Now you know what the call light has actually been about. You write his three questions on the whiteboard so the surgeon sees them at rounds.

choices.text: Reassure him the team does this procedure all the time
choices.outcome: He nods and you move on. Then he rings again at 4:00 with the same worry in different words. You never found out what he was actually afraid of, so nothing you said landed.

choices.text: Explain the procedure details yourself so he can relax
choices.outcome: You're guessing at specifics that belong to the surgeon. If what you say doesn't match what the doctor says tomorrow, he stops trusting both of you. Get his questions to the person who can actually answer them.

messages.name: DANA, CHARGE NURSE
messages.text: New admit rolling up from the ED in fifteen. You're the only one with an open bed. Also bed 8's call light has been going.

beats.prompt: Mid-conversation with a scared patient, and now this. Order of operations?

choices.text: Give Alvarez a time you'll be back, hit bed 8, then prep the admit
choices.outcome: You tell him "your questions are on the board, I'm back before 4" and he actually settles, because you gave him a real time instead of a vague one. Bed 8 turns out to be a two minute fix. That leaves ten to set up the admit room.

choices.text: Ask Dana if anyone else can take bed 8's light
choices.outcome: Fair ask, and some days she'll cover it. Today everyone's underwater, so it bounces back to you three minutes later with the patient more annoyed than before.

choices.text: Head straight to the admit room, call lights can wait
choices.outcome: Bed 8 was asking about pain medicine that was due twenty minutes ago. Now he's hurting, furious, and his daughter is at the desk asking to speak to someone in charge.

messages.name: MR. OKAFOR, BED 8
messages.text: It's not like this morning. This morning it ached. Now it's sharp when I breathe in. Something feels different.

beats.prompt: "Different." What do you do with that word?

choices.text: Ask more, look him over properly, and flag the change to Dana
choices.outcome: Sharp and new is a change, not just a number on the pain scale. You check him against this morning's notes and tell Dana it's a change from baseline and you want him seen. Maybe it's nothing. You flag it anyway, and that phrase gets attention fast on any floor.

choices.text: Give the scheduled pain med and recheck in thirty minutes
choices.outcome: The med is due and he's hurting, so nobody would blame you. Still, he told you it changed, and that part deserves a second set of eyes before you medicate it quiet.

choices.text: Chart the pain score and tell him the doctor rounds at five
choices.outcome: Two hours is a long time to sit on the word "different." If this turns out to be something real, your chart entry proves you heard him and did nothing with it.

messages.name: DANA, CHARGE NURSE
messages.text: Priya went home sick. I need you to absorb one of her patients. I know. Can you do it?

beats.prompt: You're already stretched. What do you tell her?

choices.text: Lay out exactly what you're carrying and what you can safely add
choices.outcome: "I've got a fresh admit, bed 8 waiting on the resident, and a pre-op who's anxious. I can take her if someone covers my 4 o'clock meds." Dana can juggle assignments when she has the real picture, and now she does.

choices.text: Say yes and figure it out as you go
choices.outcome: The floor appreciates it and you might pull it off. But Dana built the assignment around your yes, so by 6 you're behind on everything and nobody knows to help.

choices.text: Say yes, then vent at the nurses' station about being dumped on
choices.outcome: Everyone within earshot now knows, except the one person who could fix it. Dana would rather hear "I'm at my limit" to her face than through the grapevine at shift change.

messages.name: JEN, NIGHT SHIFT
messages.text: Okay, run your folks for me. Start with 12, he's the pre-op?

beats.prompt: Shift change. What goes in the handoff for bed 12?

choices.text: Full report, including his fear and the questions on his whiteboard
choices.outcome: Thirty extra seconds: "his brother had a bad outcome with this procedure, his questions are on the board, the surgeon hasn't addressed them yet." Jen now knows why his light will go off at 2 AM and what to say when it does.

choices.text: Stick to the clinical picture: vitals, meds, prep status
choices.outcome: Clean report, nothing wrong in it. But at 2 AM when he can't sleep, Jen starts from zero on everything you learned at 2:40 this afternoon.

choices.text: Describe him as a frequent flyer on the call light
choices.outcome: That label follows him through the night and changes how fast people walk to his room. You knew the real story behind the light, and it just got lost at the exact moment it mattered.

scenarios.debrief: Four patients, twelve hours, and most of the real work happened in ninety-second conversations between tasks. School drills the clinical skills into you; this shift tested the other half, noticing changes, saying things out loud, knowing your limits. There's no shortcut into nursing, it's an accredited program, clinicals, and board exams, and those clinicals put you on real floors sooner than you'd expect.

scenarios.title: Fourth period, sliding
scenarios.setting: 1:15 PM, fourth period algebra, right after lunch. You're ten minutes into systems of equations and you can feel the room starting to slip away from you.

messages.name: JAYLEN, BACK ROW
messages.text: Yo wait, when am I ever gonna use this? Like genuinely. Has anyone in this room EVER used this?

beats.prompt: The class laughs. He's waiting. What's the move?

choices.text: Quick real answer, keep rolling, no stage time
choices.outcome: "Fair question. Your maps app solves these every time it reroutes you. Okay, step two." Ten seconds, an actual answer, zero drama. Jaylen got acknowledged without getting a spotlight, and the lesson never stopped moving.

choices.text: Pause the lesson and open it up: why DO we learn this?
choices.outcome: A genuine discussion starts, which is lovely, and it eats eleven minutes you needed for practice problems. Some days that trade is worth it. Today it hands the room to whoever talks loudest.

choices.text: Stop everything and call out the attitude in front of the class
choices.outcome: Now it's you versus Jaylen with 28 spectators, and no teenager backs down with an audience watching. The next ten minutes belong to the standoff, and the math is gone.

messages.text: Hey. You good? You haven't touched number one.

messages.name: MAYA, SECOND ROW
messages.text: I'm fine. Just tired.

beats.prompt: Head down, worksheet blank, third day in a row. Now what?

choices.text: Shrink the task: do just the first step with her, right now
choices.outcome: You point at the first line. "Just tell me what we'd multiply here." She mumbles it. Correct. You write it down, tap the next line, and keep moving. She does the next one on her own.

choices.text: Give her space now, catch her privately after class
choices.outcome: Respectful, and the after-class talk might go somewhere. But she just spent another 40 minutes falling behind, and tomorrow the hole she's in is deeper.

choices.text: Call on her for the next answer to pull her back in
choices.outcome: She freezes, the class waits, somebody snickers. You wanted to include her and instead you confirmed her worst suspicion about this room. The head goes further down.

messages.name: JAYLEN
messages.text: Bro I'm just saying, Marcus agrees with me, this whole unit is pointless. Right, Marcus?

beats.prompt: Second disruption, and now he's recruiting. What now?

choices.text: Quiet word at his desk: a real choice, and proof you see his work
choices.outcome: You crouch next to him, voice low: "I need you working or I need you moved, your call. And you got number 3 right, so I know you can do this." No audience, a real choice, and evidence you noticed him. He picks working. Mostly.

choices.text: Clear warning with a named consequence, from the front
choices.outcome: It works for now. He stops and the class settles. But warnings from the front keep you playing whack-a-mole, and you'll be back here in about six minutes.

choices.text: Write him up and send him to the office
choices.outcome: The room goes quiet, sure. He also misses the rest of the lesson, comes back tomorrow further behind and angrier, and a kid who's behind AND bored is a bigger Tuesday problem than the jokes ever were.

messages.text: Quick check. Thumbs up if you could solve one of these on your own right now.

messages.name: PRIYA, FRONT ROW
messages.text: Honestly? I've just been copying the board. I don't actually know what we're doing.

beats.prompt: Four thumbs out of twenty-nine. Fifteen minutes left. What do you do?

choices.text: Scrap the next slide and reteach the same problem a new way
choices.outcome: You ditch the plan and redo the same problem by a different route, slower, with a kid narrating each step out loud. More hands come up. Tomorrow's pacing takes the hit and that's fine, the plan only existed to get them here.

choices.text: Finish the lesson as planned, reteach fresh tomorrow
choices.outcome: Reasonable, and the pacing guide survives. But 25 kids take tonight's homework home with a method they don't understand, and you'll spend half of tomorrow un-teaching their mistakes.

choices.text: Assign the rest as homework, they'll get it with practice
choices.outcome: They won't. The five kids with tutors will, and the gap you just widened shows up on Friday's quiz dressed up as a motivation problem.

messages.name: MAYA
messages.text: (after the bell, everyone gone) I used to be good at math. Like, actually good. I don't know what happened.

beats.prompt: She's never said this much to you. What do you say?

choices.text: Thank her for saying it and make one small, specific plan
choices.outcome: "That took guts to say. Come at lunch Thursday, bring nothing, we'll find where it broke. Ten minutes." A specific day, a small ask, no giant rescue project. She shows up Thursday.

choices.text: Tell her she's smart and it'll click again soon
choices.outcome: Kind, and she needed kind. But she told you something broke and walked away with no next step, so Thursday's class looks exactly like today's.

choices.text: Tell her she needs to participate more and keep her head up
choices.outcome: She brought you the most honest sentence she's said all semester and got a behavior note back. She won't try that again for a long time.

scenarios.debrief: That was one period out of five, and tomorrow you teach it again to a different mix of checked out, fired up, and lost. The job runs on a hundred small reads like these, made in real time, while also somehow teaching math. Public school classrooms need a credential, usually a degree plus a certification program. If today felt like a puzzle you wanted another crack at, start tutoring now; it's the same muscle and it pays while you train it.

scenarios.title: His mom booked it
scenarios.setting: 10 AM at a community counseling center. First meeting with Sam, 19, whose mom made the appointment. Your supervisor reviews your session notes afterward.

messages.name: SAM
messages.text: Just so you know, my mom made me come. I'm honestly fine. No offense, I'm sure you're good at your job or whatever.

beats.prompt: Arms crossed, eyes on the window. How do you open?

choices.text: Take the pressure off: no agenda, the hour is his
choices.outcome: "None taken. And you're not required to be un-fine in here. Since you're stuck with me for an hour, what's the story with your mom booking this?" His shoulders drop an inch and he half laughs. Then he starts talking about his mom, which means he's talking.

choices.text: Walk him through confidentiality and how sessions work
choices.outcome: He does need to hear it, and it gives him a minute to settle. But you spent the opening ten minutes in paperwork mode while he was deciding whether you're a real person. Some of that spiel could have waited.

choices.text: Point out that people who are fine don't usually end up here
choices.outcome: Technically fair, which is exactly why it lands like a trap. He goes polite and vague for the next twenty minutes, and polite and vague gives you nothing to work with.

messages.name: SAM
messages.text: She's on me constantly. Grades, my major, who I hang out with. I failed two classes last semester and now it's like I'm on trial at dinner every single night.

beats.prompt: First real thing he's offered. What do you do with it?

choices.text: Reflect it back and let it breathe
choices.outcome: "On trial at dinner. Every night." You say it back and stop. He stares at you, says "yeah, exactly," and keeps going, deeper this time. His own words coming back proved you caught it. The silence did the rest.

choices.text: Ask what happened with the two classes
choices.outcome: A reasonable thread, and you'll want it eventually. But he was telling you how home feels and you steered to transcripts. He answers your question, and the dinner-table thread goes cold for a while.

choices.text: Suggest a study system and a sit-down talk with his mom
choices.outcome: Fifteen minutes in and you're already solving. He nods along the way people nod at advice they didn't ask for, and stops handing you new material. The fast fix was never on the table anyway.

messages.name: SAM
messages.text: Okay but like, what do I do? You're the professional here. Just tell me what to do about her.

beats.prompt: He wants the answer handed over. Do you hand it over?

choices.text: Turn it back: what has he tried, and what does HE want
choices.outcome: "Before I throw ideas at you: what have you already tried? And what do you want here, separate from what she wants?" The second question stops him cold. Nobody has ever asked him it. That answer ends up running the next three sessions.

choices.text: Offer a couple of directions and let him pick
choices.outcome: A menu keeps him in the driver's seat, which is decent. But you're still the one cooking, and he walked in believing some adult always knows better. That belief is kind of the thing you're here about.

choices.text: Give him the answer: boundaries with his mom, here's how
choices.outcome: He writes it down like homework from one more adult. If it works, he learned to fetch answers from you. If it blows up at dinner, you own the blowup, and he's done with counseling at 19.

messages.name: SAM
messages.text: Sometimes I think I already wrecked it. Like everyone else figured out their thing and I burned my shot in one bad semester.

messages.name: SAM
messages.text: (goes quiet, looking at the floor)

beats.prompt: The room is silent and it's uncomfortable. What do you do?

choices.text: Let the silence sit, then reflect the feeling underneath
choices.outcome: You let it sit for what feels like a year, maybe eight actual seconds. Then: "That sounds really lonely." His eyes come up wet. This is the sentence the whole session was walking toward, and you didn't step on it.

choices.text: Normalize it: tons of people feel this way at 19
choices.outcome: True, gently meant, and it helps a little. But filing his pain under "everyone gets this" before he's finished showing it to you shrinks it. He nods and tidies himself back up.

choices.text: Jump in fast: one bad semester ruins nothing, you're fine
choices.outcome: You rescued him from the moment, and rescued yourself too, because his sadness was hard to sit near. The heavy thing goes back in the bag. It cost him a lot to take it out.

messages.name: SAM
messages.text: So... is that it? Do I come back, or what happens now?

beats.prompt: Five minutes left. How do you close a first session?

choices.text: Ask what, if anything, felt worth coming back for
choices.outcome: He thinks, then says "the what-do-I-want question, I guess." So that becomes next week's thread, his pick. You book it, remind him what stays confidential, and flag the family dynamics for your supervisor review.

choices.text: Book the standard weekly slot and recap the session
choices.outcome: Clean and professional, and he'll probably show. But the appointment belongs to the calendar instead of to him, and with a kid who got marched in here, whose idea this is matters a lot.

choices.text: Send him off with a list of exercises for the week
choices.outcome: Homework from another adult, the exact dynamic he spent an hour describing. The list lands in his notes app, unopened, right next to the guilt about it.

scenarios.debrief: An hour of mostly not talking, and you're somehow more tired than after a workout. That's the actual job: holding the room steady so someone can finally hear themselves think. Getting licensed takes graduate school plus supervised hours, so it's a long road, but peer support roles let you start practicing the listening part years earlier.

scenarios.title: The deal went quiet
