scenarios.setting: Tuesday morning, pipeline review in an hour. Meridian Logistics loved your demo three weeks ago. Then Priya, your champion there, stopped answering.

messages.name: PRIYA (3 WEEKS AGO)
messages.text: This demo was great. Let me socialize it with my team and circle back next week!
Hey Priya, just checking in on next steps!

beats.prompt: That check-in was six days ago. Still nothing. What do you send?

choices.text: Send something useful: a one-pager on the dock delays she mentioned
choices.outcome: You rebuild the note around her own words from the demo: the dock delays costing her team nights and weekends. Reply lands in four hours: "ok this is exactly our problem. Call Thursday?" You gave her a reason to answer that had nothing to do with your quota.

choices.text: Short and honest: has this dropped off your list? No hard feelings
choices.outcome: The classic takeaway note, and it works often enough to keep in the toolkit. She does reply. But you spent your one re-entry move on a yes or no about the deal instead of on her problem.

choices.text: Offer 15% off if she signs by Friday
choices.outcome: Discounting into silence tells her two things: the price was padded, and you're the one feeling pressure. If that email reaches procurement later, every number you quote gets a haircut.

messages.name: PRIYA
messages.text: Sorry for the ghost. Still very interested. Honestly the holdup is my boss Marcus. He thinks we can keep limping along on spreadsheets.

beats.prompt: The real blocker has a name now. Your move?

choices.text: Ask what Marcus actually objects to, and what would move him
choices.outcome: Discovery on the blocker. Turns out Marcus got burned by a tool rollout in 2023 and the spreadsheet thing is cover. Now you and Priya are planning how to answer his real concern together. She ghosted you three weeks ago; today she's co-writing the plan.

choices.text: Send her your ROI deck to forward to Marcus
choices.outcome: The deck is decent and she forwards it. But a forwarded PDF argues with nobody. You still don't know what Marcus's actual objection is, so the deck answers a question he may not even be asking.

choices.text: Ask for Marcus's email so you can pitch him directly
choices.outcome: You just told your only ally that her role is over. Priya goes cold, Marcus ignores the stranger in his inbox, and now there is nobody inside that building pulling for you.

messages.name: MARCUS (ON THE CALL)
messages.text: I'll be straight with you. We brought in a platform like this two years ago. Six figures, big promises, and my team was back on spreadsheets within a quarter.

beats.prompt: The decision maker just showed you his scar. What now?

choices.text: Ask what went wrong last time before you say anything
choices.outcome: He talks for four minutes: no training, no internal owner, vendor vanished after signature. You take notes. Every word is a spec for how to win this account, and he's visibly surprised anyone bothered to ask.

choices.text: Explain the three ways your product is different
choices.outcome: A fine answer to the surface objection. But you're differentiating against a product you know nothing about, from a failure you haven't heard the story of. Some of your three points land. You're guessing which.

choices.text: Tell him that vendor is famous for overpromising
choices.outcome: Trash talk feels like taking his side and reads like a rep covering for his whole category. What Marcus hears is "you got fooled," and the man who signs this deal does not enjoy hearing that.

messages.name: PRIYA
messages.text: Marcus is warming up. Last thing: the quote. He saw the number and said, and I'm quoting directly, "that's a lot for software."

beats.prompt: Price objection, secondhand. How do you handle it?

choices.text: Ask a lot compared to what, then price out doing nothing
choices.outcome: "Compared to what?" turns out to mean compared to free spreadsheets. So you do the math with her: the dock delays run about $9k a month in overtime. Set against that, the quote reads very differently, and nobody dropped a cent.

choices.text: Walk through what's included and why it costs what it costs
choices.outcome: Professional, and the number stays intact. It half lands. Justifying your price is fine; anchoring it against their $9k a month problem would have been stronger, and you had the ammo in hand.

choices.text: Come back with 20% off before anyone asks twice
choices.outcome: You negotiated against yourself. Marcus, a man who buys things for a living, immediately wonders what an actual push would get him. The number is officially soft now, and the real negotiation starts below it.

messages.name: YOUR MANAGER (SLACK)
messages.text: Meridian. Can it sign by the 30th? I have it in commit for the quarter.

messages.name: PRIYA
messages.text: Realistically, legal review puts us mid next month. That's the honest timeline.

beats.prompt: Quarter end says this week. The customer says next month. What do you do?

choices.text: Build a close plan with Priya, forecast it honestly as next month
choices.outcome: You and Priya map every step with dates: legal, security review, signatures. Your manager pulls it from commit, annoyed for about a day. It signs on the 12th, exactly on plan, and next quarter your forecasts get taken at face value.

choices.text: Ask once if an end-of-quarter incentive speeds up legal
choices.outcome: Worth one ask, as long as you take the first no. Priya checks; legal is legal. You spent a little goodwill to confirm the timeline was real, and at least you didn't push twice.

choices.text: Tell Priya the pricing expires on the 30th, take it or leave it
choices.outcome: Fake urgency on a real champion. She's been straight with you the whole way and can smell that the deadline is yours, not hers. Her reply is one line: "Then pull it." Enjoy explaining that in pipeline review.

scenarios.debrief: Three weeks of a deal compressed into two minutes, and notice how little of it was pitching. Mostly you asked one more question and told the truth about timelines. Sales has no degree gate; it runs on proof, call recordings, pipeline stories, quota history, which means you can start stacking evidence in a part-time sales job this year.

scenarios.title: Everyone wants a date
scenarios.setting: 9:30 AM and Slack is already busy. The CSV export feature you spec'd is supposed to anchor the Q2 release, and the eng lead just finished reading the spec.

messages.name: ROSA (ENG LEAD)
messages.text: Read the spec. That's three sprints minimum. The export piece alone touches the old billing code, and that code is haunted.

beats.prompt: Your one-sprint feature just tripled. First response?

choices.text: Ask her to walk you through where the cost actually lives
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes at a whiteboard. Turns out 80% of the pain is one thing: scheduled exports hitting the haunted billing tables. A one-time manual export is cheap. You can't make a smart cut until you can see the map, and now you have the map.

choices.text: Ask what she'd cut to get it down to one sprint
choices.outcome: Efficient, and Rosa has opinions. But you're handing a product decision to whatever happens to be annoying to build, and the cheapest version is not automatically the version users need.

choices.text: Remind her the scope was committed in planning
choices.outcome: She goes quiet in the way engineers go quiet right before they stop telling you things. The scope stays "committed" and arrives three weeks late anyway, except now you find out at the deadline instead of today.

messages.name: ROSA
messages.text: So yeah. Manual export is clean, one sprint. Scheduled exports means going into billing. That's the three-sprint monster.

beats.prompt: Where do you draw the cut line?

choices.text: Ship manual export now, make scheduled its own decision later
choices.outcome: You rewrite the cut line in the PRD: v1 is manual export, scheduled becomes its own project with its own go or no-go. Support tickets show most users export monthly anyway. Rosa commits to the sprint without flinching.

choices.text: Keep the full scope and push the release date out
choices.outcome: Honest, at least, and occasionally right. But the thing users beg for weekly, any export at all, now waits nine weeks behind a scheduler that a handful of power users asked for once.

choices.text: Ask if a quick hacky version of scheduled export fits
choices.outcome: Rosa's face does a thing. A hack inside haunted billing code is how you end up with a 2 AM incident carrying your feature's name, and she will remember exactly who asked her to plant it there.

messages.name: DEREK (VP SALES)
messages.text: Hey! Northstar Corp keeps asking when export goes live. I'm seeing them Thursday. What date can I give them?

beats.prompt: A VP wants a date and he wants it now. What do you give him?

choices.text: Give a range, your confidence level, and what ships first
choices.outcome: "Manual export: first week of May, high confidence. Scheduled: being scoped, real answer in two weeks." Derek walks into Thursday with something true to say and nothing you'll have to walk back later.

choices.text: Tell him you'll confirm after sprint planning on Friday
choices.outcome: Careful, and sometimes right. Except Thursday comes before Friday, Derek still needs a sentence for that room, and a VP with no sentence will improvise one. You will not like the improv.

choices.text: Give the optimistic date, April 15, the team can stretch
choices.outcome: Derek repeats it to Northstar within the hour, probably in writing. You just converted a stretch goal into a customer commitment, and the team that has to eat it wasn't in the room.

messages.name: DEREK
messages.text: Two weeks to scope?? Come on. Just tell them June 1 for the scheduled thing. Worst case we're a little late, they'll live.

beats.prompt: He's pushing. Do you bend?

choices.text: Hold the line: commit to an answer date, not a ship date
choices.outcome: "I won't give a date I can't back. What I can promise: a real answer by the 19th, and you get the first call." Derek grumbles and takes it. A quarter later he's telling other VPs your dates are the ones that hold.

choices.text: Loop in your manager to settle it
choices.outcome: Escalation is a real tool and sometimes the right one. Spend it here, though, and Derek learns that pushing you summons a tiebreaker. You had the standing to hold this one yourself.

choices.text: Fine, June 1, worst case it slips a little
choices.outcome: It slips. Northstar's renewal call lands two weeks after the missed date, and the slide titled "vendor misses commitments" has your feature on it. Derek, naturally, remembers the date and forgets the pressure.

messages.name: ROSA
messages.text: Heads up. Two days out, QA found exports silently dropping rows on accounts with 10k+ records. Maybe 2% of customers. Ship or hold?

beats.prompt: Two days to launch. Ship or hold?

choices.text: Size the blast radius with her, hold if the data can lie quietly
choices.outcome: Silently wrong data is the worst kind, because customers paste it into real decisions before anyone notices. You check who's in the 2%: three of your ten biggest accounts, Northstar included. You slip four days, ship clean, and nobody outside the team ever knows.

choices.text: Hold a full week across the board to be extra safe
choices.outcome: Safe, and nobody gets hurt. But you never asked how big the blast radius actually was, so you bought the maximum delay without pricing the smaller one. Fine outcome, loose reasoning.

choices.text: Ship it, 2% is edge case territory, patch next sprint
choices.outcome: The 2% includes Northstar. Their ops lead builds a quarterly report on quietly wrong numbers, finds out from a support ticket, and Derek gets the angriest email of his month. So do you.

scenarios.debrief: No code written, no pixels pushed, and you still made six calls that decided what ships, when, and whether anyone trusts the dates. That's the job: judgment, out loud, in writing, all day. There's no single doorway in, PMs arrive from engineering, design, and support, and what gets you hired is evidence of that judgment: a sharp PRD, a shipped experiment, a cut line you can defend.

scenarios.title: Is it actually ready?
scenarios.setting: 2 PM launch review. The team built an AI assistant that answers customer billing questions. The demo is gorgeous. The call on whether it ships is yours.

messages.name: THEO (ENG LEAD)
messages.text: Demo killed with the exec team. We're at 82% on our test set. Marketing wants to announce Friday. Green light?

beats.prompt: 82% and a Friday deadline. What's your first question?

choices.text: Ask what the 18% looks like before touching the launch question
choices.outcome: You ask for the ten worst failures, not the average. Three of them are the bot confidently stating a refund amount that doesn't exist. An 82 that fails politely is shippable; an 82 that fails confidently about money is a different animal, and now the whole room can see which one this is.

choices.text: Ask Theo to push accuracy to 90 first
choices.outcome: A number for a number. The team grinds on the metric, but nobody has asked whether the remaining failures are harmless or horrible, and a 90 that invents refund amounts is the same problem wearing a nicer score.

choices.text: Green light, the demo was great and the execs are hyped
choices.outcome: A demo is the model on its best day with a driver who knows the roads. Real users arrive with typos, rage, and questions nobody wrote down. You're about to discover the gap between demo and field in public.

messages.name: NADIA (DESIGN)
messages.text: Pulled the failure examples. When it's wrong it is SO confident. Same cheerful tone telling you a refund that doesn't exist is on the way.

beats.prompt: Confidently wrong about money. What does "ready" mean now?

choices.text: Set launch criteria by failure type, design the uncertain state
choices.outcome: You write it on the board: hedged-and-wrong is tolerable, confident-and-wrong about money is a launch blocker, and below a confidence threshold the bot says "let me get a human." Nadia starts designing the handoff. Now "ready" is something you can actually test.

choices.text: Add a disclaimer: AI can make mistakes, verify important info
choices.outcome: Legal will love it. But a disclaimer hands quality control to the user, and the person asking about their refund at 11 PM is the least equipped person in the building to catch the bot lying cheerfully.

choices.text: Keep demos to the question types it handles well
choices.outcome: That curates the demo and leaves the product untouched, and the gap ships to users either way. Also the team sees what you did, and quietly recalibrates how much your launch bar actually means.

messages.name: MINA (DATA SCIENCE)
messages.text: Small confession. The test set is 60 questions we wrote ourselves in a doc. Real users might phrase things... differently.

beats.prompt: Your 82% just got shakier. How do you fix the eval?

choices.text: Pull real support tickets, rebuild the eval on actual user language
choices.outcome: Two days mining real tickets produces an eval set full of typos, half-questions, and anger, which is to say, reality. Accuracy drops to 71 on the first pass. Painful number, honest number. From here, improvements actually mean something.

choices.text: Have the team write 300 more synthetic questions
choices.outcome: More coverage of how your team imagines users talk. The set gets bigger while the blind spot keeps its exact shape. Better than 60, still a mirror.

choices.text: Have everyone try to break it for an afternoon and call it tested
choices.outcome: The red-team afternoon is fun and finds a few gems. But five people who built the thing can't un-know how it works. They probe where they already expect weakness, and real users will arrive from every other direction.

messages.name: CARLA (VP PRODUCT)
messages.text: Competitor announced their version this morning. CEO is asking why ours isn't out. I need a launch posture by tomorrow.

beats.prompt: Competitive pressure just landed on your timeline. What's the posture?

choices.text: Propose a 5% beta with monitoring and written kill criteria
choices.outcome: You bring a one-pager: 5% of traffic, human handoff live, dashboards on wrong-answer rate, and the exact numbers that trigger a rollback. Carla can defend that upstairs because it has teeth. You're shipping Friday after all. Just not to everyone.

choices.text: Commit to a full launch in three weeks, fixes included
choices.outcome: A real plan with a real date, and Carla takes it. But it's all-or-nothing in three weeks with zero field data in between, and the bet rests on the eval set you just learned to distrust.

choices.text: Match the competitor, full launch Friday
choices.outcome: Their launch, your deadline. Within a week, screenshots of the confident refund bot are circulating, and support is drowning in tickets about the feature that was built to reduce tickets. The competitor's bot being equally bad helps nobody.

messages.name: THEO
messages.text: Week one beta data. Common billing questions: 94%, humans barely needed. Refund-status questions from annual-plan customers: 61%, and the misses are ugly.

beats.prompt: Strong on common cases, weak on one segment. Now what?

choices.text: Ship where it's strong, route the weak segment to humans, say so
choices.outcome: The bot keeps the common questions it nails, and annual-plan refund queries skip straight to a person. The launch copy says exactly that: most billing questions handled, humans cover the rest. The 61% becomes next quarter's project with real traffic data behind it.

choices.text: Hold everything until the weak segment clears the bar
choices.outcome: Principled, and sometimes right. But thousands of users who'd get great answers today keep waiting on the hardest segment's schedule, and your fastest route to fixing it, real traffic, stays switched off.

choices.text: Launch broad, annual-plan is a small slice anyway
choices.outcome: Small slice, highest-paying customers. The people spending the most money get the worst bot, which is exactly the kind of sentence that shows up in a churn postmortem with your launch doc linked.

scenarios.debrief: Nobody in that room asked you to write code. They asked you to decide what good enough means for a system that is sometimes confidently wrong, and to hold that line through a demo high and a competitor's press release. The role usually grows out of PM, engineering, or research, and the fastest way to prove you can do it is what you just did: a PRD with failure modes, and an eval scorecard that says in numbers when to ship.

scenarios.title: Launch week wobble
scenarios.setting: Monday, 8:50 AM. Your app launch goes live at noon: paid ads on two channels, a creator partnership as the centerpiece, and a CEO who refreshes dashboards for sport.

messages.name: JUNO (CREATOR, 1.2M FOLLOWERS)
messages.text: hey so. the script your team sent. I love the app but I cannot say "revolutionize your routine" with a straight face. my audience will clock it in two seconds.

beats.prompt: Your centerpiece partner hates the script, hours before launch. Response?

choices.text: Send 3 must-hit points and let her write it in her own voice
choices.outcome: You reply with three bullets: the feature to show, the promo code, the one claim legal needs intact. "Everything else, your voice." Her draft lands that night, sounds nothing like your script, and is better. She has 1.2 million people precisely because she knows what they'll clock.

choices.text: Get on a call and walk through why each line matters
choices.outcome: She takes the call, she's a pro. You rescue two lines and burn an afternoon of launch day, and the final read still carries a faint hostage-video energy that her comment section will absolutely notice.

choices.text: Hold firm, the script cleared legal and brand review
choices.outcome: She posts it exactly as written, with the enthusiasm of a court statement. Top comment: "she's so getting paid for this." Technically compliant, a dead asset, and one creator telling her group chat your brand is a pain to work with.

messages.name: DIEGO (YOUR BOSS, SLACK)
messages.text: CEO wants launch numbers for his 4pm. What do we have?

beats.prompt: Three hours of data, none of it clean. What do you send up?

choices.text: Send what's real, labeled early: signups, source, what's unknown
choices.outcome: "3 hours in: 1,840 signups, 60% from Juno's audience, paid still in learning phase, CAC means nothing before Wednesday." Diego forwards it word for word, caveats and all. The CEO's read is that marketing has its hands on the wheel.

choices.text: Ask to hold reporting until tomorrow when the data's clean
choices.outcome: Analytically correct, and tomorrow's number will be more real. But the 4pm happens with or without you, and the CEO fills the silence with whatever the dashboard half-tells him, minus your caveats.

choices.text: Send the flashiest cut: impressions up 400%
choices.outcome: The CEO repeats it at 4, someone asks "400% of what," and now Wednesday's report has to walk back Monday's headline. Impressions are the easiest number to inflate and the first one a board member discounts.

messages.name: KWAME (ANALYST)
messages.text: Day 2 paid check-in. Instagram CPA $11, on target. TikTok CPA $46 against a $12 target. Kill TikTok?

beats.prompt: One channel is bleeding. Kill it, feed it, or wait?

choices.text: Go one level down: which creative, which audience is dragging it
choices.outcome: Ten minutes in the ads manager: two of the three TikTok creatives are fine, and the expensive polished one is eating 70% of spend with zero conversions. You kill that one ad and shift its budget to the scrappy UGC-style spot. By Thursday, TikTok's CPA is $14 and falling.

choices.text: Pause TikTok, move the budget to Instagram
choices.outcome: Defensible triage, and Instagram absorbs the spend fine. You also learned nothing about why TikTok failed, so next launch you get to pay for this same lesson at full price.

choices.text: Leave it alone, day 2 is early, the algorithm needs to learn
choices.outcome: Learning phase is a real thing, which is what makes this tempting. But $46 against $12 is a quarter of your launch budget burning while you wait politely. By Friday the money's gone and the lesson costs exactly the same.

messages.name: KWAME
messages.text: Uh. Juno's video is live. 290k views in 2 hours. It's also missing the promo code, and she tagged @yourapp_ instead of @yourapp.

beats.prompt: Viral and broken at the same time. What's the fix?

choices.text: Friendly fast ask: fix the caption, pin a comment with the code
choices.outcome: One warm message, zero blame: "video's crushing! can you fix the tag in the caption and pin the code in a comment?" Done in 20 minutes, momentum untouched, and the pinned comment ends up converting better than the caption would have. Relationship intact for launch number two.

choices.text: Ask her to take it down and repost it corrected
choices.outcome: She does it, a little stung. The repost loses the early momentum the algorithm had already rewarded and restarts at zero against the morning's 290k. You fixed the metadata and paid for it in reach.

choices.text: Correct it publicly from the brand account in her comments
choices.outcome: Correcting a partner in her own comments reads as a slap in front of 290k onlookers. Her audience piles in to defend her, the story becomes "brand embarrasses creator," and the video everyone is watching is now about that.

messages.name: DIEGO
messages.text: Friday wrap for the exec team. Where do we land?

beats.prompt: Mixed week: signups beat target, CAC missed it. How do you tell it?

choices.text: Tell it straight: the win, the miss, the cause, the week-two fix
choices.outcome: One slide: 9,400 signups against a 7,000 target, blended CAC $19 against $15, cause traced to TikTok's dead creative, fix already live. Two execs ask sharp questions and you have answers because you did the digging on Tuesday. Budget for phase two clears by end of day.

choices.text: Lead with the wins, keep CAC in the appendix
choices.outcome: Everyone enjoys the meeting. Then the CFO finds CAC in the appendix on his own time, and the question becomes why it was in the appendix. The miss was survivable. The placement turned it into a thing.

choices.text: Blame TikTok's algorithm and the creator's tagging mistake
choices.outcome: Maybe partly true, totally useless. You hired the channel and sent the script, so the room hears it as a dodge. The CAC miss would have been forgotten by Monday. The dodge follows you into Q3 planning.

scenarios.debrief: Five days: one partnership saved twice, one ad channel rescued by a ten-minute dig, and a numbers story told straight to the people holding the budget. Launch weeks run on exactly this mix of creative taste and spreadsheet nerve. Degrees help at big brands, but startups hire off proof: a campaign you actually ran with real numbers attached, and a tiny one for a club or a friend's shop counts.

scenarios.title: The Monday export
scenarios.setting: 8:51 AM, Monday. The weekly KPI email goes out at 10, and the export you just pulled says signups fell off a cliff.

beats.prompt: Signups down 38%. What do you check before anything else?

choices.text: Whether checkouts and revenue dropped too
choices.outcome: They didn't. People are still buying, and you can't check out without an account, so the signup number and the revenue number can't both be true. Revenue reconciles against the bank, which makes signups the suspect.

choices.text: Rerun the export in case the job pulled a stale table
choices.outcome: Worth 30 seconds, and it comes back identical. A clean rerun only proves the pipeline agrees with itself. It says nothing about whether the tracking underneath is healthy.

choices.text: Slack the growth lead right now so nobody's blindsided
choices.outcome: By 9:20 there's a war room, a theory about the new landing page, and a designer getting pulled off another project. Walking that back costs more than the ten minutes a sanity check would have.

beats.prompt: iOS is fine. Here's web, day by day. What is this shape?

choices.text: Zero events after a Thursday deploy smells like broken tracking
choices.outcome: Real demand never hits literal zero on a Saturday, even terrible products get a few stragglers. A flatline that starts hours after a release points at the code that fires the event, so you pull the release notes.

choices.text: Compare against the same week last year for seasonality
choices.outcome: Reasonable reflex, and last October does show a dip, about 4%. Nothing seasonal takes a metric to zero though, so you're back staring at that Thursday within ten minutes.

choices.text: Take it at face value: the Thursday redesign scared users off
choices.outcome: You build a deck about form friction while the actual signup event sits renamed in the codebase. Two weeks of design fixes later, someone in engineering finds it by accident.

beats.prompt: There it is. What do you do with it?

choices.text: Tell eng and the growth lead together, with the proof attached
choices.outcome: Eng patches the event name by lunch and growth stands down before anyone ships a fix for a problem that never existed. You also ask for a backfill estimate, because the dashboard has a four-day hole either way.

choices.text: File a bug ticket with the diff and get back to your queue
choices.outcome: The fix lands eventually. Meanwhile the 10 AM email is still due, the number is still wrong, and the growth lead learns about it from the ticket queue instead of from you.

choices.text: Patch your dashboard query to count both event names, quietly
choices.outcome: Your chart heals. Every other query in the company that touches sign_up stays broken, and three teams ship decisions on it before anyone connects the dots.

beats.prompt: It's 9:56. How does the email go out?

choices.text: Corrected number, plus the note on what broke and what's pending
choices.outcome: Nobody panics, and when the raw tables shift during Wednesday's backfill, nobody is surprised either. You flagged it first, which is exactly what keeps forty people trusting the same number.

choices.text: Hold the email until the backfill lands Wednesday
choices.outcome: Defensible, but the company runs its Monday meetings on this email. Three days of silence breeds more rumors than one asterisk ever could.

choices.text: Send the original export, correct it next Monday
choices.outcome: Someone screenshots the minus 38 for an all-hands slide before your correction lands. You spend the next two weeks finding every copy of that number and killing it.

scenarios.debrief: A lot of this job is exactly that: a number looks wrong, and you get to find out whether the business changed or the measurement did. The SQL is learnable in months. The instinct to cross-check before you sound an alarm takes longer, and it's what hiring managers actually screen for. A degree helps, but a public repo with one real dataset, a clean dashboard, and an honest memo opens most of the same doors.

scenarios.title: The 9 AM page
scenarios.setting: 9:14 AM. You're on call this week, and the checkout crash channel started pinging before you found a desk.

beats.prompt: The trace says price.ts line 41. Where do you actually start?

choices.text: Ask what changed around 09:02 before touching any code
choices.outcome: formatPrice has shipped unchanged for two years. A line that worked yesterday and crashes today means its input changed, so the real question is what started feeding it garbage this morning.

choices.text: Open price.ts:41 and read the function
choices.outcome: You read it: it formats price.amount, exactly like the trace says. Five minutes confirming the crash site is honest work, but this function did nothing wrong. Something upstream handed it an undefined.

choices.text: Add a null check at line 41 and ship it
choices.outcome: The crash count drops to zero and so does your visibility. Carts now silently render without prices, support tickets start at 11, and the real bug is still in there with the alarm unplugged.

beats.prompt: Three recent deploys. Which one gets your attention?

choices.text: cart-svc v212: new caching, live right before the first crash
choices.outcome: Shipped at 09:00, first crash at 09:02, and it changed how cart data gets served. Timing plus data path beats everything else on the list.

choices.text: Reproduce it locally with your own test cart first
choices.outcome: Solid instinct on a normal day. Your local setup has no cache in front of it though, so everything works perfectly, and twenty minutes are gone while prod keeps counting.

choices.text: web v4.9.1, the crash is in frontend code after all
choices.outcome: You diff it: a banner string changed. It's easy to chase the deploy that lives where the stack trace points, but copy changes don't make objects undefined.

beats.prompt: Same endpoint, two different answers. What's the bug?

choices.text: The new cache serializer drops the nested price object
choices.outcome: Cache misses return full objects, hits return amputated ones. price.ts:41 was innocent the whole time. The frontend just happened to be the first thing to trip over the hole.

choices.text: Harden the frontend to show a placeholder when price is null
choices.outcome: Reasonable armor to add later, and some teams would. Right now it treats the symptom while every cache hit keeps serving broken carts to anything else that reads them.

choices.text: Null price means free, patch formatPrice to show $0.00
choices.outcome: A cart full of $0.00 items looks like a pricing catastrophe, and screenshots of it are on social media by noon. Worse than the crash you started with.

beats.prompt: Errors still climbing. What ships first?

choices.text: A: roll back to v211, fix the serializer calmly afterward
choices.outcome: Four minutes later the graph flatlines at zero. Rollback first, root cause second is the on-call playbook at most shops: get back to the known-good version, then fix the real thing without a timer running.

choices.text: B: flush the cache for instant relief
choices.outcome: Errors drop in 30 seconds, then creep back as the cache refills through the same broken serializer. You bought minutes, and now the graph is confusing on top of everything else.

choices.text: C: write the real fix now, rollbacks feel like admitting defeat
choices.outcome: Forty-five minutes of coding under pressure, plus review, plus deploy, while thousands more carts crash. The elegant fix can wait until the site works.

scenarios.debrief: Notice how little of that was typing code. Some weeks debugging is most of the job: reading evidence, distrusting the obvious suspect, picking the boring fix while a counter climbs. A CS degree helps, but what gets you hired is proof you can ship and reason like this: a deployed project with tests, a README, and a write-up of something that broke and how you found it.

scenarios.title: The number that's too good
scenarios.setting: Tuesday morning in the lab. The overnight viability assay just finished, and one number in the readout is about to test your self-control.

beats.prompt: Compound C, rep 1 looks like a monster hit. First reaction?

choices.text: Look hard at C's other two reps before believing rep 1
choices.outcome: 64.8 and 66.2 agree with each other and disagree with 12.3 completely. When one replicate screams and its siblings shrug, you investigate the screamer, and the first suspect is the well it lived in.

choices.text: Queue a fresh rerun of compound C right away
choices.outcome: Rerunning is the right destination, but you'd burn cells and a day without knowing why rep 1 diverged. The plate map might answer that in thirty seconds.

choices.text: Text the PI: compound C kills 88% of the cells
choices.outcome: She forwards it to a collaborator before lunch. When the number dies under scrutiny, and numbers like this usually do, you get to write the correction email to people you've never met.

beats.prompt: Rep 1 lived in a corner well. What killed those cells?

choices.text: Evaporation. Corner wells dry out, and dead cells read as a hit
choices.outcome: Edge wells lose volume fastest, the medium concentrates, and cells die of thirst instead of chemistry. Every screening lab has a story about an edge-well breakthrough. Now you have yours.

choices.text: Can't rule out a real effect yet. Flag it, redo in interior wells
choices.outcome: Careful, and nobody would fault you. With the lid log and the corner position, though, the artifact explanation already fits every data point, so design the redo around it: interior wells, edges filled with media only.

choices.text: Drop the two boring replicates, rep 1 is the interesting data
choices.outcome: Choosing your favorite replicate has a name in this field, and careers end over it. The notebook keeps all three numbers forever, whatever you decide to report.

beats.prompt: Modest, real, and dose-dependent. How does it go in the notebook?

choices.text: Full entry: run 15 results plus the run 14 artifact, documented
choices.outcome: The dose response is the finding, and the edge artifact goes in the record with the lid log attached. Six months from now when someone asks why run 14 looks weird, the answer is already written down.

choices.text: Write up run 15 and leave run 14 out, it was just an artifact
choices.outcome: Cleaner story, and plenty of people do it. But an unexplained ugly run sitting in the raw data with no notebook entry is exactly what makes a reviewer start pulling threads.

choices.text: Average all six replicates across both runs for a better n
choices.outcome: You just mixed a known artifact into a clean dataset to inflate your sample size. Any statistician who sees the raw plates will take the whole analysis apart.

beats.prompt: The PI needs something exciting by 5. What goes on the slide?

choices.text: The dose response with error bars, pitched as a lead worth chasing
choices.outcome: A real 35% effect at 30uM with clean stats is a fundable lead. PIs can sell honest and promising, and she'd much rather defend a modest true number than explain a flashy one that collapses in review.

choices.text: Ask for two more weeks to run a proper confirmation first
choices.outcome: Rigorous, but the deadline is real and run 15 already replicates with dose dependence. Knowing when data is solid enough to show is its own skill, and this clears the bar.

choices.text: The 12.3% from run 14, it's technically a recorded data point
choices.outcome: It is, with a documented artifact attached to it. If a reviewer requests the raw data, that slide turns the renewal from a funding question into an integrity question.

scenarios.debrief: A lot of research weeks look like this one: a thrilling readout on Tuesday, a smaller true answer by Friday, and a notebook that has to hold both. If picking apart your own result felt satisfying instead of deflating, pay attention to that. Entry runs through a degree, usually a graduate one, and you can start the evidence trail now: replicating a published experiment on public data is the classic first proof.

scenarios.title: Ship it? The v9 question
scenarios.setting: Wednesday, 2 PM. Your retrained ticket router beats the old model on the eval you've stared at for three weeks, and the PM wants a launch date.

beats.prompt: Overall accuracy is up 2.4 points. Ready to ship?

choices.text: No. Refunds dropped 13 points, find out why first
choices.outcome: Refunds is where angry customers and chargebacks live, so a 13-point hole there can cost more than 2.4 aggregate points buy. Aggregate numbers smooth over exactly this kind of hole, which is why the report breaks out slices at all.

choices.text: Ship to 5% behind a flag and watch the live numbers
choices.outcome: A canary is a legitimate tool and plenty of teams would start here. You already have the warning offline though. Sending real refund customers into a known weak spot to reconfirm it is an expensive second opinion.

choices.text: Ship it. The team OKR tracks overall accuracy and this crushes it
choices.outcome: Three weeks later, escalations from refund customers are up 40% and the model gets rolled back in a hurry with your name on the launch doc. The OKR looks great the entire time.

beats.prompt: What's actually going on in that slice?

choices.text: v9 never saw the new refund policy language, so it reads billing
choices.outcome: The September policy changed the words customers use, and v9's training data ends in August. The slice drop has a concrete cause and a concrete fix: get current refund tickets labeled and into the training set.

choices.text: Suspect label noise and send the slice back for relabeling
choices.outcome: Labels do rot, so it's a fair guess. But 31 of 40 errors landing in the same wrong bucket with the same token is too organized for noise. Random noise scatters across buckets instead of piling into one.

choices.text: Add a rule: any ticket containing 'chargeback' routes to refunds
choices.outcome: Works in the demo. Then 'I never filed a chargeback, why is my card charged' routes to refunds, paraphrases slip past, and six months later nobody remembers the regex quietly overriding the model.

beats.prompt: The PM wants a launch date Friday. What do you pitch?

choices.text: A, with the slice table as the reason the week is worth it
choices.outcome: You put 71.3 next to the support cost of one misrouted refund, and the PM moves the date without much of a fight. Most PMs will trade a week for not shipping a known customer-facing hole, as long as you bring numbers instead of vibes.

choices.text: C: split routing as a bridge while the labels get collected
choices.outcome: Workable, and teams really do this. You're now running two models, two monitoring paths, and a split somebody has to remember to tear down later. It holds up as a short bridge if the labeling actually stays on schedule.

choices.text: B: fine-tune on refunds tonight, re-eval in the morning
choices.outcome: Morning results: refunds up to 88, billing down 6, tech issue down 4. Narrow fine-tunes love to pay for one slice with three others, and now you're debugging that with two days left.

beats.prompt: v10 is green everywhere. Last move before full rollout?

choices.text: Add fresh refund-slice cases to the standing regression suite
choices.outcome: Twelve cases is thin for the slice that just burned you. The next policy change will try the same trick, and after today the suite checks every future retrain against the exact failure you spent a week fixing.

choices.text: Roll out and babysit the dashboards for a week
choices.outcome: You'd catch a repeat this month. Vigilance works while it lasts, but in a month you'll be deep in the next project, and whatever watches this slice then won't be you.

choices.text: Delete the v8 fallback path today, dead code is tech debt
choices.outcome: A week later a bad config push tanks v10 and there's nothing to fail over to. The escape hatch stays until the new thing has survived something real.

scenarios.debrief: Training the model was maybe a tenth of what you just did. The job lives in eval tables, slice checks, labeling plans, and deciding what's safe to ship, and a pager goes off when you guess wrong. Degrees help here, but a deployed system with a real eval suite and honest metrics can carry you in. Build one end to end, training to serving, and write down its failure modes: that write-up is the interview.

scenarios.title: Passing on a technicality
scenarios.setting: 10:30 AM. You're reviewing last night's eval run for the support bot ahead of Thursday's release. Case 47 is marked green.

paper.title: EVAL CASE 47  AUTO: PASS
lines: user: 'so do i get my money

beats.prompt: The suite says PASS. Do you?

choices.text: No. It committed to a refund, just without the trigger words
choices.outcome: The customer now believes money is coming, which is the exact harm the rule exists to prevent. The regex tested the wording while the model made the commitment in fresh vocabulary.

choices.text: Flag it as borderline and ask the policy owner to rule on it
choices.outcome: Getting a ruling is fair, and the answer will be what you already suspect. The sharper question you'd be sitting on in the meantime: how many of the other green checkmarks look like this one.

choices.text: Green is green. 400 more cases before Thursday
choices.outcome: Reasonable throughput math, wrong week for it. The bot tells a customer money is coming, the money doesn't come, and the complaint lands on an exec's desk with a transcript attached and PASS stamped on it.

beats.prompt: 23 false passes. Fix the model first or the grader first?

choices.text: The grader. Until it can see failures, no fix is verifiable
choices.outcome: Any prompt change you make now gets scored by a checker that misses two-thirds of the problem, so you couldn't tell whether a fix worked or just moved the failures somewhere the regex doesn't look.

choices.text: The model. Tighten the system prompt against promising outcomes
choices.outcome: A fair instinct, and the prompt probably does need it. But you'd be verifying the fix with the same grader that just missed 23 of these, so the confidence you end up with is fake.

choices.text: Neither, hand-review all 412 transcripts yourself tonight
choices.outcome: You'd catch everything, once. Next week's run has 412 more, every prompt tweak triggers a rerun, and a plan that needs a heroic all-nighter per release dies by the third release.

beats.prompt: The judge hits 46 of 50. Ship it as the release gate?

choices.text: Ship it, and keep the 50 labeled cases as a check on the judge
choices.outcome: Judges drift like anything else, so the calibration set becomes a standing test. If judge-human agreement slips after someone swaps the judge model version, you find out from a number instead of from an incident.

choices.text: Ship it as is, 92% agreement beats 62% by a mile
choices.outcome: It does, and shipping is right. Shipping with nothing watching the judge is the gap: six months from now the judge gets quietly upgraded and nobody notices the rubric stopped landing.

choices.text: Keep tuning the judge prompt until it scores 50/50 on this set
choices.outcome: You can absolutely hit 50/50, by teaching the judge these 50 answers. On case 51 it performs worse than the version you started with. Overfitting applies to judges the same as to models.

beats.prompt: Three fails out of 412. What do you walk into the 3 PM review with?

choices.text: The three transcripts and a severity read on each
choices.outcome: A 99.3% pass rate means nothing without knowing what's in the 0.7%. 'Billing will approve it' is a promise with a specific department attached, and the room needs to see it verbatim to price the risk.

choices.text: The pass rate, with a one-line note that fails exist
choices.outcome: Accurate, and the review probably waves it through. You've also made the severity call for everyone else by compressing it into a footnote, and nobody got the chance to disagree with you.

choices.text: A quick prompt patch now so the number reads 100% by 3
choices.outcome: An untested prompt change two hours before a release gate, verified by a single rerun. Sometimes it holds. The time it doesn't, the postmortem timeline reads 'edited the prompt at 1 PM, shipped at 4.'

scenarios.debrief: You spent that whole shift judging the judges, which is most of what this job actually is: the model fools the test, so you build a better test, then check who's testing the test. The title is new enough that nobody agrees on required credentials, which cuts in your favor. A versioned prompt library, a rubric raters actually agree on, and a catalog of failures you fixed will beat a resume line almost everywhere.

scenarios.title: Where the orders pile up
scenarios.setting: Tuesday, 8 AM, the fulfillment warehouse office. Orders are shipping late, the GM blames packing, and you've got a timing sheet and a walkie.

beats.prompt: The GM wants two more packers approved today. Do you sign off?

choices.text: Not yet. 46 orders are stacked at label, go look at that station
choices.outcome: Pack takes the longest per order, but ten packers run in parallel. One label station is a funnel everything squeezes through, and the 46-order pile is the floor telling you where it hurts.

choices.text: Ask for another week of data before deciding anything
choices.outcome: More data rarely hurts, but the queue column is already screaming. A week of confirming it costs a week of late orders, and the GM stops inviting you to the meetings where things get decided.

choices.text: Sign off, 8.2 minutes is clearly the slowest step
choices.outcome: Two hires later, packed orders reach the label queue even faster and the pile grows to 60. You sped up the step before the clog. Late shipments don't move at all.

beats.prompt: Orders wait 19 minutes for a 2-minute step. The cheap fix?

choices.text: Attack the single station: a second printer, or printers at pack
choices.outcome: Doubling capacity at the constraint roughly doubles what the whole line can ship, and a label printer costs less than one week of the overtime this backlog burns. Nothing upstream matters until this station can swallow what pick and pack feed it.

choices.text: Put a floater on jam duty so the one printer stays up
choices.outcome: Uptime climbs to maybe 90% and the queue shrinks some. You've made one printer less fragile, but one printer is still the ceiling on the entire building's output.

choices.text: Tell pick and pack to push harder and clear the backlog
choices.outcome: They can go faster, and the pile at label grows faster. By Thursday there are carts of unlabeled orders blocking the aisles, and the late count is worse than when you started.

beats.prompt: You get ten minutes with the GM. What's the pitch?

choices.text: Option A, with the 46-order queue as exhibit one
choices.outcome: A $2,400 printer buying 70% more throughput, against $110k a year of packers buying 3%. When the numbers are this lopsided, your job is mostly making sure the room actually sees them side by side.

choices.text: A and B together, cover both bases in one ask
choices.outcome: The printer still does all the work in that bundle. You've attached $110k a year of padding to a $2,400 fix, and a sharp GM will ask which half you actually believe in.

choices.text: C, the warehouse system fixes this properly and forever
choices.outcome: Four months and $60k to solve what a printer solves on Thursday. Big-system proposals feel thorough, and the queue sits there growing the whole time you're writing the RFP.

beats.prompt: Throughput up 43%. Where does your attention go now?

choices.text: The loading dock. The pile moved, so the constraint moved
choices.outcome: Fixing one constraint promotes the next one, and loading is already showing the same pattern label did. Start timing the dock now, while the queue is 22 and annoyed instead of 60 and on fire.

choices.text: Write up the win and present it before touching anything else
choices.outcome: Do document it. Credit matters, and so does the before-and-after story. But if loading blows up while you're polishing slides, the win you're presenting is already stale.

choices.text: Nothing. Close the project, the bottleneck is fixed
choices.outcome: Three weeks later orders run late again and the GM asks why the fix stopped working. It didn't. The 22 orders sitting at the dock were on your own report.

scenarios.debrief: You just watched a timing sheet point at the wrong culprit, which happens constantly in this job. The work is following the queues instead of the opinions, then persuading someone with a budget to act on what you found. Entry is genuinely mixed: spreadsheets, a mapped process, and one before-and-after fix you can show go further than most credentials.

scenarios.title: $14.70, every month
scenarios.setting: Month-end close, day two. The bank rec is off again, and the gap has been growing by the exact same amount for three months.

beats.prompt: The gap grows by exactly $14.70 every month. What is that?

choices.text: A recurring charge the books never see. Hunt a monthly $14.70
choices.outcome: Identical amount, identical direction, stacking by one unit a month: that's a subscription or a bank fee hitting cash with no journal entry behind it. Random errors don't repeat to the penny.

choices.text: Ask the senior if under-$50 differences can sit in suspense
choices.outcome: There is a threshold, and the senior would probably say yes. You'd also be teaching yourself to stop looking at a pattern that took ten seconds to spot, and suspense balances have a way of growing.

choices.text: Plug it to misc expense and close, it's immaterial
choices.outcome: It ties, this month. Auditors pull plug entries first, and a plug that grows by $14.70 each month reads less like immaterial and more like nobody looked.

beats.prompt: A canceled vendor, still pulling money. What now?

choices.text: Book the fees properly and start recovery on all three charges
choices.outcome: Two problems, two fixes: the books need the expense recorded either way, and the company is owed $44.10 plus whatever October pulls if nobody blocks the ACH. You chase both, in writing.

choices.text: Book the expense and set a reminder to watch for October's
choices.outcome: The rec ties, and charge number four arrives October 3 right on schedule. You've scheduled yourself to witness a leak you could have ended today.

choices.text: Call the bank to dispute it, skip the journal entries
choices.outcome: Maybe the dispute wins in a few weeks. Meanwhile the books still don't match the bank, the rec still doesn't tie, and the close is still stuck on day two.

beats.prompt: July and August are closed periods. How do you book their $29.40?

choices.text: Catch-up entry in September, with a memo telling the whole story
choices.outcome: Reopening two closed months over $29.40 costs far more than it's worth, and a catch-up entry is the standard move for immaterial items. The memo is what makes it clean: anyone who finds JE #0912 in April understands it in one read.

choices.text: Take it to the controller and let her make the call
choices.outcome: Never wrong to escalate, and she says exactly what you suspected: book it in September with a clear memo. No harm done, though this one was inside your authority.

choices.text: Book only September's $14.70, prior months are history
choices.outcome: The rec is still off by $29.40, and the trail is muddier now, because the one entry that exists suggests someone looked and stopped. Next month's version of you inherits the mystery with fewer clues.

beats.prompt: The rec ties. What's worth adding so this never happens again?

choices.text: A control: canceling a vendor must include revoking ACH access
choices.outcome: The contract got canceled but nobody told the bank, and that gap stays open for every future vendor until the offboarding checklist closes it. One checkbox on a form ends this entire category of leak.

choices.text: A recurring task to scan bank activity for canceled vendors
choices.outcome: A decent detective control, and it would catch the next one within a month. It still spends your hours catching what a one-line change to the cancellation process would prevent.

choices.text: Nothing. It was $14.70 and it's handled
choices.outcome: This vendor is handled. The process that let a canceled contract keep billing is untouched, and the next one might pull $1,400 a month instead.

scenarios.debrief: Reconciliation sounds like box-checking until a $14.70 thread leads you to a hole in the process that nobody knew was open. That's the real texture of the job: small numbers, actual stakes, and a monthly rhythm you can get genuinely good at. The road in usually runs through an accounting degree, with the CPA as a bigger unlock later, though bookkeeping work can get you started earlier than either.

scenarios.title: The sev2 at 2:07
scenarios.setting: 2:07 PM. The latency pager for the AI assistant goes off mid-bite of your lunch, and the provider's status page has a convenient excuse ready.

beats.prompt: The provider status page says it's them. Do you buy it?

choices.text: Not yet. Cost tripled too, and their slowness can't spend your money
choices.outcome: A slow provider makes the same tokens arrive later. Spending 2.6x means you're sending or retrying more than you were an hour ago, and that points back inside your own system.

choices.text: Fail over to the backup provider now, sort out blame after
choices.outcome: A real lever, and sometimes the right first pull. If the problem is your own payload, though, it follows you to the new provider at the same bloated cost, and now you've changed two things mid-incident.

choices.text: Post 'provider issue, monitoring their status page' and wait
choices.outcome: Comfortable, and it buys an hour of silence while the queue grows. When their page goes green and your latency doesn't move, you restart the investigation an hour deep in backlog.

beats.prompt: What actually happened at 13:45?

choices.text: context-svc started stuffing full chat history into every call
choices.outcome: Four times the input tokens per request, deployed 22 minutes before the page. The provider is processing at the same speed it always does. You're asking it for four times the work, and the status page blip was a coincidence.

choices.text: The provider is throttling the bigger payloads
choices.outcome: Plausible theory, but ms/token sitting flat at 24 all day argues against it. Throttling shows up as slower service, and this is the same service doing a much bigger job.

choices.text: Upgrade to the faster, pricier model tier to absorb the load
choices.outcome: Latency improves a little, cost goes from $310 an hour to $700, and the actual bug ships itself into next week's baseline. You'd be paying a premium to avoid reading a deploy log.

beats.prompt: Queue's at 2,140 and climbing. First move?

choices.text: A: roll back to the version that worked this morning
choices.outcome: Five minutes to a state you've already seen behave. The flag is faster, but it's new behavior nobody tested, and mid-incident is a bad time to discover what a 10-turn cap does to long support conversations.

choices.text: B: flip the flag, it's live in one minute
choices.outcome: It probably works, and one minute is tempting with the queue climbing. You're shipping untested behavior into an incident though, and if truncated context degrades answers, you now have two overlapping problems to untangle.

choices.text: C: bump the alert threshold so the pager stops screaming
choices.outcome: The paging stops. Users still wait 12 seconds, the queue still grows, and the money still burns at $310 an hour. You've treated the one part of the incident that was working correctly.

beats.prompt: Postmortem's tomorrow. Which action item actually prevents a repeat?

choices.text: Alert on tokens per request, and check it in deploy canaries
choices.outcome: Latency told you something was wrong 22 minutes late. A tokens-per-request alert would have fired inside the canary window, before full rollout, with the guilty deploy standing right next to the graph.

choices.text: Require an ops review for any change touching prompts or context
choices.outcome: Catches some of these, at the price of making you the person every team waits on. It also relies on a human spotting what a canary metric would catch automatically.

choices.text: Write 'engineers should double-check context changes' in the doc
choices.outcome: The doc gets nodded at and filed. Six weeks later a different service quadruples output tokens instead, and nothing pages until users complain, because 'be careful' was never going to fire an alert.

scenarios.debrief: That was one pager out of a rotation full of them: half detective work, half plumbing, with real money on the meter the whole time. Nobody has a degree in this yet, which is your opening. A cost dashboard you built, an eval harness that catches regressions, and one honest incident write-up make the portfolio that gets you the interview.

scenarios.title: The rail that sags
scenarios.setting: Thursday afternoon at the bench. Board rev B, unit 3, and the 3.3 volt rail is fine right up until you ask it to do anything.

beats.prompt: 3V3 drops 0.4 volts under load. First move?

choices.text: Probe 3V3 right at the regulator pin, under the same load
choices.outcome: Before blaming any part, find where the voltage is actually lost. If U4's own pin holds near 3.3 under load, the regulator is doing its job and the drop lives somewhere along the path. Ten minutes of probing beats a week of swapping parts on a hunch.

choices.text: Pull the U4 datasheet and check its current limit
choices.outcome: Worth knowing, and it's rated for 3A, so 1.5A shouldn't strain it. That rules out one theory but still doesn't tell you where your 0.4 volts went.

choices.text: Swap U4, weak regulators are a known thing
choices.outcome: Forty minutes of hot-air rework later, the new regulator sags the exact same 0.4 volts. The part was never the problem, and unit 3 now has a reworked footprint that complicates every measurement after this.

beats.prompt: There's the map. Where is the 0.4 volts going?

choices.text: Mostly across J5, plus the run after it. Resistance in the path
choices.outcome: The regulator holds 3.28 right at its pin, then the voltage bleeds away through the connector and the downstream trace. Ohm's law doing exactly what it does: 0.22 volts at 1.5 amps is about 150 milliohms hiding in a connector.

choices.text: J5 looks bad, but check L2 for saturation while you're in there
choices.outcome: Thorough, and saturation is a real failure mode. L2 is only dropping 20 millivolts though, so you'd be splitting attention between a paper cut and the open wound at J5.

choices.text: Add bulk capacitance at the far end to prop the rail up
choices.outcome: Caps ride out spikes and transients. This is a steady-state drop across real resistance, so the new caps charge up to the same sagging 2.91 and sit there. Day lost, problem identical.

beats.prompt: 140 milliohms against a 20 spec. Bad design or bad part?

choices.text: Swap in a fresh J5 and re-measure before judging the design
choices.outcome: The fresh connector reads 18 milliohms and the sag shrinks to 60 millivolts. This sample was simply worn out, mated 200 times on a 30-cycle rating. Bench abuse, not a design flaw, though one pin carrying all the power deserves a second look anyway.

choices.text: Assume design margin is thin and start the rev C changes now
choices.outcome: You might land on the right changes, but you'd be revising a board based on one worn sample. If the real story is 200 mating cycles on a 30-cycle part, your rev C change gets credit for a fix it didn't make, and the test report says something false.

choices.text: Solder a jumper wire across J5 and move on with bring-up
choices.outcome: Unit 3 works great now. Units 1, 2, and every production board still carry the open question, and the jumper means this unit can no longer tell you anything true about the connector.

beats.prompt: The change request is drafted. What goes in the review packet with it?

choices.text: The bench data: idle vs load readings and the full probe walk
choices.outcome: Reviewers approve evidence faster than opinion. The probe walk shows exactly where every millivolt went, why two pins and a fatter trace fix it, and why the worn connector muddied the first reading. The whole argument fits in one table.

choices.text: Just the calculation, the numbers make the case on their own
choices.outcome: The math is right, and Vance might sign off. The first question in review will still be 'what did you measure,' and 'it's in my notebook somewhere' lands a lot worse than a page in the packet.

choices.text: Skip the formal review, it's two pins and a wider trace
choices.outcome: Small changes to power delivery have a long history of surprising people. If the wider trace crowds something near it, or the second pin changes a part number downstream, the first person to find out shouldn't be the factory.

scenarios.debrief: A sagging rail, a probe, and an afternoon of narrowing down where the volts went: that's a very normal Thursday in this field. The satisfaction is real, and so is the patience it takes. Entry runs through an EE degree almost everywhere, with the PE license mattering later for public and consulting work, but a documented project like this one, requirements to schematic to test data, is what makes a resume read like an engineer wrote it.

scenarios.title: Cutoff day, two short
scenarios.setting: 12:40 PM at a regional fulfillment site. The afternoon wave just dropped, and the UPS trailer at dock 3 pulls out at 3:00 whether you're ready or not.

beats.prompt: Wave 14 just dropped. Where do you point people first?

choices.text: Get a lift driver replenishing A-14 before pickers reach that aisle
choices.outcome: Replen first. An empty bin mid-wave turns thirty picks into thirty exceptions, and exceptions eat a lead's whole afternoon. You clear the thing the wave is about to run into, then release the pickers.

choices.text: Release the pickers now, handle A-14 when somebody hits it
choices.outcome: The wave moves, which feels right. But the first picker to hit A-14 radios you, then the next one, and now you're fixing it anyway with a line of carts stacked behind the problem.

choices.text: Unload trailer 4412 first, that driver's been sitting 35 minutes
choices.outcome: Detention fees sting, but nothing on that inbound trailer ships today. Wave 14 ships at 3:00 or it doesn't ship at all. Keep the driver posted and keep your people on the wave.

beats.prompt: Deanna and Marcus just called out. Zone B is down to one picker.

choices.text: Move two packers up to Zone B, flex them back when cartons stack
choices.outcome: Pick feeds pack. If picks stall, the pack line starves in twenty minutes anyway, so you borrow from downstream and send them back once the queue builds. Leads shuffle people like this all shift long.

choices.text: Call the morning shift, ask who wants four hours of overtime
choices.outcome: A real lever, and sometimes the right one. But the soonest anyone walks in is 1:45 and your gap is right now. Make the call, sure, just move bodies first.

choices.text: Grab a cart and pick Zone B yourself, you're fast
choices.outcome: You pick eighty units and nobody runs the floor for two hours. The board drifts, exceptions pile up, and the next problem finds no one watching for it. A lead on a cart is a picker, not a lead.

beats.prompt: A picker radios: something's leaking under a pallet in B-07, and carts are still rolling through it.

choices.text: Stop traffic in the aisle, cone it off, ID the liquid before cleanup
choices.outcome: Aisle closed, carts rerouted, and you check the pallet's paperwork before anyone touches the puddle. If that's degreaser instead of water, the cleanup changes completely. You lose fifteen minutes of Zone B, and that trade is never close on this floor.

choices.text: Close all of Zone B until it's cleaned and documented
choices.outcome: Nobody gets hurt, which is the whole point. But one aisle was the hazard, and you just parked four pickers for the worst half hour of cutoff day over one wet aisle.

choices.text: Have them throw spill pads over it and keep the picks moving
choices.outcome: Pads on a liquid you haven't identified, with carts rolling through at wave pace. If someone goes down there, the cutoff stops mattering instantly. A comp claim and an OSHA log entry cost more than every order on this wave.

beats.prompt: 2:35. Twenty-four orders left and the trailer pulls at 3:00. Nine of them are next-day air.

choices.text: Re-cut the list: air orders first, ground rolls to tomorrow if needed
choices.outcome: The nine air orders carry promised dates. The ground orders have a day of slack. You pick the nine, pack them hot, and whatever ground makes it makes it. Triage like this is most of the job after lunch.

choices.text: Call the UPS driver and ask for a 20 minute hold on the pull
choices.outcome: Drivers say yes to this maybe half the time, and it costs you a favor. Worth trying after you've re-sequenced, not instead of it. If he says no, you're right back here with less clock.

choices.text: Rally everyone to push all 24, tell them to hustle
choices.outcome: Rushing a tired, short-handed crew at 2:35 is where mispicks and jammed fingers come from. You'll load 24 boxes and spend tomorrow processing returns on three of them. Pick fewer orders correctly.

beats.prompt: 3:20. Trailer's gone with every air order on it. Night lead clocks in at 4. What's left for you?

choices.text: Write the B-07 report now, then walk the night lead through the board
choices.outcome: You write it while the details are fresh: what leaked, who was near it, what you did about it. If a picker wakes up tomorrow with a rash and there's no report, that becomes a very different conversation. Then the handoff happens face to face, not on a sticky note.

choices.text: Get trailer 4412 unloaded first and cut the driver loose
choices.outcome: Detention is real money and somebody should get on that unload. But the night crew can empty a trailer. Only you can write down what you saw in B-07, and memory goes soft by tomorrow.

choices.text: Jump in and help pack the rolled ground orders
choices.outcome: Those fifteen orders ship fine at 8 AM without you. Meanwhile the spill never gets documented and the night lead inherits a board nobody explained. The last hour of a lead's shift is paperwork and handoff, and it matters more than it looks.

scenarios.debrief: That was one wave on one shift, and tomorrow's board will break somewhere different. The job is people, clock, and freight all moving at once, and the floor grades your plan within the hour. Most leads started on a cart and got noticed for fixing flow, not just surviving it. Start anywhere on the floor, write down what's broken, and bring a flow map and a shift checklist when the lead spot opens.

scenarios.title: Blast radius
scenarios.setting: 9:05 AM on a Tuesday, mid-sprint. You open the board before standup and two pings are already waiting for you.

beats.prompt: Three things before 9:30. What do you pull first?

choices.text: Chase the API spec: find out why it slipped and who it's stalling
choices.outcome: The spec has two teams idling behind it, and every hour it slips the stall spreads. The deck is four hours away and it's one person's afternoon. You rank by how many people each problem takes down, then by the clock.

choices.text: Start the VP deck, 1:00 is the only hard deadline on the board
choices.outcome: Defensible, and plenty of coordinators would. But a deck written at 9:15 describes a slip you haven't investigated yet. Go learn what's true first and the deck half writes itself at 11.

choices.text: Clear Marco's design pass, it's a quick review
choices.outcome: Ten minutes, one green checkmark, and the spec got ten minutes older. Marco's pass was due Thursday. It could have waited until Thursday.

beats.prompt: Priya levels with you: she's also on a prod bug, and the spec needs two more days.

choices.text: Ask her which endpoints are stable, publish a draft so mobile can stub
choices.outcome: Priya says the auth and charge endpoints won't change, so a draft goes out by 10 and mobile starts building against stubs. Two days of full stall just turned into a half speed Tuesday, which the plan can absorb. A lot of this job is finding the piece that's already solid and shipping that.

choices.text: Escalate to her manager, get her pulled off the prod bug
choices.outcome: Sometimes right, and the manager should hear about the collision either way. But you're spending capital to move a problem sideways: the prod bug lands on someone else, and Priya remembers who escalated. Try the cheap move first.

choices.text: Push the due date out two days in the tracker and post the update
choices.outcome: The tracker is accurate now, and three mobile engineers are exactly as stuck as they were. A date change records the slip. Somebody still has to go work it, and that somebody is you.

beats.prompt: 11:40. The VP's EA pings: she wants the full deck, with the payments timeline. You have about 40 usable minutes.

choices.text: Send three slides: status, the slip, the recovery plan already running
choices.outcome: One slide per thing that matters, the slip named plainly, the fix shown right next to it. Execs at 1 PM want to know what's wrong and who's on it. Nobody in that room has ever asked for more slides.

choices.text: Block the full 40 minutes and build the complete deck she asked for
choices.outcome: You'll walk in with a polished deck, and that's not nothing. But you went dark for 40 minutes mid slip, and if mobile hit a snag at noon, nobody was answering. The deck was never the risky item on your board today.

choices.text: Mark payments yellow with 'mitigation in progress' and keep it vague
choices.outcome: The VP finds out Thursday what the slip actually was, and from then on she reads all your greens as maybes. You want her bored reading your updates, never surprised.

tickets.item: CSV export, new ask from Sales

beats.prompt: 2:30. The sales lead calls, loud and friendly: tiny ask, a CSV export for Friday's demo, the team can squeeze it in, right?

choices.text: Get an engineering estimate, then show the sponsor what it displaces
choices.outcome: The estimate comes back at four days, which means the reporting dashboard moves. You put that trade in front of the sponsor as a choice, not a complaint. About half the time the ask quietly disappears once it has a price tag.

choices.text: Hold the line: nothing enters mid sprint, offer next sprint's slot
choices.outcome: By the book, and the team will love you for it. The catch is you decided alone that Friday's demo doesn't matter, and sales escalates over your head tomorrow with no numbers on your side. Price it first, then hold the line with the price.

choices.text: Say yes, it does sound small, and the team always finds a way
choices.outcome: Mid sprint adds land on whoever can't say no, and this one lands on Priya, the person holding your riskiest deliverable. The spec slips a third day and now both problems have your name on them.

beats.prompt: 5:15. Everything's stable and nothing's finished. Last move before you log off?

choices.text: Send a short update: what moved today, what gets decided tomorrow
choices.outcome: Five lines to the right people: spec draft is out, deck landed fine, CSV call comes from Dana by 10. Nobody refreshes a tracker at 9 PM wondering what's true. Tomorrow starts with everyone holding the same picture.

choices.text: Update the tracker and build tomorrow's standup agenda
choices.outcome: Clean and useful, and the tracker should reflect today. But a tracker only tells people what changed if they go look. The reporting team might not look tonight, and they're the ones whose work might move.

choices.text: Sit on the reporting news until Dana actually decides tomorrow
choices.outcome: If the dashboard moves, that team hears about their own work last, from a tracker diff. People forgive a slip. Finding out late, from the tool instead of from you, is the part that sticks.

scenarios.debrief: You built nothing today, and the sprint still lives or dies on the calls you made before lunch. The job is carrying the whole picture so eight other people can go deep on one piece each. Most coordinators come up through ops or admin work, and certifications help, but calm delivery and a clean tracker are what actually get you hired. Build the tracker kit and run a mock retro on a project that went sideways; that's your proof.
